speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order, although perhaps Your Honour may be inclined to call it a grievance. It is a point of order in that it points out what 1 consider to be a very serious deficiency in our rules with respect to the examination of estimates. I refer specifically to Standing Order 58(14) under which all estimates are deemed to have been reported back to the House as of midnight, May 31. Because of limitations of space, and because we have difficulty manning committees, House committees now operate under what is known as a block system. Consequently, committees have to plan their schedules in such way as to ensure that there is adequate time to examine estimates as well as legislation.
The committee that is charged with the responsibility of examining the estimates of the Ministry of State for Urban Affairs is the omnibus committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs. In addition to examining the estimates of the Ministry of State for Urban Affairs, it is also charged with examination of estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare, the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, and a number of commissions and agencies, including the National Capital Commission, the Medical Research Council of Canada, and so on.
My point of order is the following: While Standing Order 58(14) states that the estimates are deemed to have been reported back to the House by midnight, May 31, there is nothing there that states that estimates have to be examined by a committee. So all a minister has to do is to hold fast with one excuse after another if, in fact, he does not want to have the estimates of his department examined by the committee.
I believe that such a situation is developing with respect to the estimates of the Ministry of State for Urban Affairs, and specifically the estimates of the Crown corporation for which the minister answers, which is CMHC. That independent Crown corporation spends over $600 million a year. It is a very important Crown corporation. Indeed, it is just about the total responsibility of the Ministry of State for Urban Affairs.
Business of the House
Yesterday, notwithstanding the fact that a meeting today had been scheduled for the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs to examine the estimates of the Ministry of State for Urban Affairs, the chairman of the committee was called to cancel the examination of the ministry because the minister was not able to attend. The chairman had to comply, and a notice went out cancelling today's meeting.
My understanding is that Crown corporations, by tradition and practice of the House, appear before committees without the benefit of the minister who answers for them being present. In other words, committees should be able to proceed, whether or not the Minister of State for Urban Affairs is present, with an examination of the estimates of CMHC. Our problem is that we have evidence before us which we have ventilated in the House. We have gone as far as we can go with it in the House. Indeed, we have an admission from the minister that the whole procedure of the administration of that part of the National Housing Act will be tightened up. We had an admission from him that the National Housing Act has been used improperly in terms of funding by way of guaranteed loan hotels. There is no provision in the act anywhere, especially in that section of the act which is being invoked for this reason, namely, section 6(1), to give authority to CMHC or the Ministry of State for Urban Affairs, or anybody else, to provide guaranteed loans for hotels. We know there are two hotels which the minister has admitted were funded in this way. One of them is the subject of bankruptcy proceedings. That is how the whole thing came out. Twelve such hotels have been so funded in Canada since 1973. That happens to coincide with the time Mr. William Teron became the president of CMHC. In addition to holding down that position, he is now undersecretary of the Minister of State for Urban Affairs, or the deputy minister.
For the balance of this month, the schedule of meetings of the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs is such that there will be only two occasions on which the committee will have an opportunity to examine the $600 million worth of estimates of CMHC. The committee is scheduled to meet tomorrow morning, and because of the meeting being pre-empted by the question period at 11 a.m. we will have only an hour and a half, or less, tomorrow morning. The next meeting is scheduled for May 5, which means that we will have two meetings, or a total of approximately six hours, to examine the $600 million estimates of CMHC, the National Capital Commission and all the other responsibilities of the Minister of State for Urban Affairs.
I can almost anticipate what Your Honour is going to say. There is reference on the order paper to reactivating the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization, but in my opinion there is, if not a question of privilege, a very serious grievance here in that hon. members of this House are being deprived of their right and, indeed, their responsibility properly to examine estimates prior to voting on the supply bill. The frustration was not only that we could not confront the minister and his department in committee, but the minister has a very definite responsibility in the province of Quebec right now, and he has not been in the House either. Because of the failure of the government to live up to its commitment and to implement some of the other parts of the program, we need to know under what jurisdiction these loans were made and how much they have cost the Canadian taxpayer.
The thing which really offends me-and my colleague touched on it-is that yesterday we were informed that the Minister of State for Urban Affairs will not permit the chairman of the board of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the deputy minister of urban affairs, to appear on his own before the committee. I can sympathize with the minister, particularly in light of press reports with respect to the conduct and the character of this senior public official, namely, William Teron. That conduct was challenged in the court and the court ruled against the government, so 1 can understand that the minister would be nervous about allowing this senior official to appear before the committee on his own. speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member for St. John's East has raised, by way of a point of order, a rather serious matter. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext:
In connection with the very interesting point of order raised by the hon. member for St. John's East, hon. members will be aware that one of the constant grievances of the past has been the fact that the House, under any system, has had to come to a point where in order to allow for orderly planning of federal governmental affairs it had to vote a supply of money to the government. That moment has arrived in the past and has been troubled by the appearance of members of the House of Commons receiving at the very last
April 28, 1977

minute, on the last allotted day, a supply bill upon which they have been asked to vote. Even the appearance of voting that amount of money in a short time is a little unsavoury.
The explanation and the understanding for that is that the decisions really are not made at the last moment, although the bill cannot be produced for the scrutiny of all hon. members until that time. In fact, the amounts are known and the make up and every page, line and comma of those bills can be predicted in advance because of the system under which the estimates are referred to the standing committees; and hon. members are given the opportunity to examine and question ministers on those spending estimates. Therefore, it is justified that hon. members are asked to vote supply on the last day, because they have had that opportunity, in the interval, to give thorough examination to the spending estimates.
In fact, we have been able to use that system since the beginning of this parliament in order to progress a little and, I am happy to say, to release the supply bill earlier in the day so that we are all given the opportunity to absorb its contents a little in advance. That takes away the strain of being presented with the bill only moments before the vote.
The functioning of the entire system is predicated on the theory that opposition members indeed, members on all sides of the House are given a proper and adequate opportunity in the intervening period between the introduction of the estimates and the introduction of the supply bill to examine ministers on their spending estimates in the standing committees. Indeed, the point of the hon. member for Selkirk is well taken in that respect. One recognizes that a meeting may have to be postponed for the convenience of important witnesses who are to appear. After all, every member of this House works under a heavy schedule. Such postponements can be understood.
While the point raised may not at the moment constitute a question of privilege or point of order, the Chair can surely not do otherwise than look on the matter most seriously as striking at the fundamental roots of the right of every member to function properly. Any step which might be viewed by the public as jeopardizing the full and complete right of any member to examine a minister upon his spending estimates before a committee must be viewed seriously.
Therefore, within the limits of good will and co-operation it is expected that as a fundamental part of the entire system any minister owes it to the House and to the country to extend his utmost co-operation in facilitating committee meetings, in appearing there and in making sure that all officials necessary for the proper examination of the estimates appear with him.
The whole argument in past years for this system of the examination of spending estimates is that certain advantages exist in standing committees which do not exist in committee of the whole. That is to say, in standing committees several sets of officials may accompany the minister, and if questions on peripheral issues have to be raised at the time itis not necessary to go to another committee meeting: questions may
Report of Clerk of Petitions
be put to, and answers obtained from the minister or his officials, or the minister may answer through his officials, which may be the proper parliamentary function. Certainly, the presence of officials who can advise and counsel the minister is an important part of the exercise.
I do not question the right of any minister to say that his responsibilities ought to be borne by himself, but I do say, again-to make the point clear, if it is not clear already-that the point raised does not constitute, in its present form, a point of order or a question of privilege, because any cancellation or postponement may not have been of such an extent as to exhibit any ill will or attempt, however unwitting or accidental, to frustrate the system. If that has not existed up to the present time, then perhaps these remarks are simply nothing more than an admonition or description of what in the opinion of the Chair is expected of a minister in these circumstances.
To make the point perfectly clear, it seems to me to be fundamental to the entire system that a minister shall be expected to be seen to extend to the House the utmost co-operation and assistance in facilitating the most meaningful examination of his spending estimates in the standing committees in every way possible.

subsubtopic: LAETRILE
speechtext:
1.	Does the government have objections against the establishment of Cancer Control Centres such as those in Mexico where a product called Laetrile is used and, if so, what are they?
2.	What procedures would have to be followed to obtain approval to establish such a Cancer Control Centre in Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: LAETRILE
speechtext:
1. The government of Canada does not object to the establishment of Cancer Control Centres. There are many Cancer Control Centres or clinics in Canada; however, the use of Laetrile is not permitted in Canada. Since 1963, scientists of the Department of National Health and Welfare have examined and evaluated periodically all the available information and material on Laetrile supplied by the manufacturer or obtained from other sources. As a result of these repeated examinations, the department has concluded that it cannot permit Laetrile to be distributed in Canada and that it shares the position on this drug taken by two of the most important medical bodies in fighting cancer in Canada. The National Cancer Institute of Canada has expressed extreme concern about the publicity purporting to show therapeutic value for Laetrile, on the basis that this drug is of no proven value. Therefore, the institute considers that promotion of this drug may constitute a cruel fraud at least, and even be harmful by delaying or preventing access to treatment of known value. An identical position has been taken by the Canadian Medical Association. (See the News Release issued by the Department of National Health and Welfare on May 20, 1975.)
2.	The use of Laetrile in cancer control centres in Canada would require the submission of acceptable evidence of the efficiency and safety of this agent. No drug manufacturer has ever filed a satisfactory submission providing acceptable evidence of the efficacy and safety of Laetrile, which would be required in order to permit the marketing of this drug in Canada.

April 28, 1977

1975-82; May 20, 1975; Departmental Position on Alleged Cancer Drug: Ottawa-National Health and Welfare Minister, Marc Lalonde, today made public the position of his department on a so-called cancer remedy known under the name Laetrile. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation rebroadcast a special program on its English television network, on Sunday, May 18, 1975, where this drug was presented as a useful weapon against cancer. Mr. Lalonde said that taking into account all known facts, the Health Protection Branch cannot permit Laetrile to be distributed in Canada and that it shares the position on this drug taken by two important medical bodies involved in fighting cancer in Canada. The National Cancer Institute of Canada has evinced extreme concern about publicity purporting to show therapeutic value for Laetrile, on the basis that this drug is of no proven clinical value. Therefore, the Institute considers that the promotion of this drug may constitute a cruel fraud at least, and even be harmful by delaying or preventing access to treatment of known value. An identical position has been taken recently by the Canadian Medical Association. Laetrile-or amygdaline- is a substance obtained from defatted apricot kernels by extraction and recrystallization. It has been stated by its proponents that the drug reacts with an enzyme in excess in cancer tissue, producing hydrogen cyanide to which cancer cells are sensitive. No drug manufacturer has ever filed a satisfactory submission to market this drug in Canada. In March 1964, in order to stop an illegal Canadian distribution of Laetrile, the then Food and Drug Directorate seized all available supplies. The directorate's action was upheld by Superior Court in Quebec, which said that it would be far more dangerous to suspend a law intended to safeguard the health of the general public than to deprive certain patients from acquiring a drug of dubious value that had not been tested for safety and effectiveness. The 1964 situation still exists and the drug is still considered of dubious value. Preliminary studies conducted on animals at the Sloan Kettering Institute, a well-known cancer institute in the United States, have shown that there was some slight suggestion of benefit in tumour-bearing animals. The scientists who conducted these studies do not believe, however, that the animal data are sufficiently promising to indicate the value of a clinical trial with Laetrile. In 1966, following a careful review of the literature and investigations by the Cancer Commission of the California Medical Association and this department, the American Cancer Society stated it had found no evidence that treatment with Laetrile results in any objective benefit in the treatment of cancer in human beings. No information to the contrary has become available since then. It seems that most if not all of the clinical evidence presented for Laetrile is based on the uncontrolled subjective impressions of only a few physicians. There has been testimonial information claiming cases of improvement in some patients, but their long-term health status, whether any effects could validly be attributed to Laetrile, or how many patients given Laetrile subsequently died, are not known. Mr. Lalonde emphasized that he and his officials are as anxious as cancer patients and their families to see the marketing of an effective cancer drug, but that he does
Order Paper Questions
not believe marketing of a remedy should be permitted without sound scientific evidence as to its safety and effectiveness. Mr. Lalonde also regretted that despite representation from his department, the Canadian Medical Association and the National Cancer Institute, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation chose to rebroadcast a program which could raise false hopes about the value of Laetrile in the treatment of cancer.

I am informed by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation as follows: it is not a requirement of the by-laws of the CBC that meetings of the board of directors be held in camera, or privately. One of those attributes is the holding of private meetings of its board of directors. The effectiveness of the board's frank discussions of matters of internal management and administration would be lessened if its meetings were held in public. The public is represented by the board of directors whose members are chosen from the various geographic regions of Canada and from various walks of life. In fairness to the minister, on the point of order I may say that the addition of a preamble at the report stage of a bill raises, if not procedural concerns at least some comment that a preamble, by its very terms, is something that comes before the bill and not after. Regardless of its merit, it is an extraordinary circumstance. It certainly has been examined several times in British practice. It has been found that a preamble cannot be added at the committee stage, in the precedents that are applicable. Since it obviously is not appropriate as a second-reading amendment, the effect of that ruling is that it cannot be introduced as an amendment to the bill which, frankly, troubles me somewhat. Some bills have preambles, and others do not. One has to start from the basic premise that a member probably has the right somewhere along the line at least to attempt to introduce a preamble into bills that do not have preambles-provided the preamble is otherwise procedurally correct.
Whether that can be done at report stage raises some misgivings, but under existing precedents it cannot be done any sooner. There are procedural questions we ought to settle.
I am not certain, in the circumstance, whether unanimous consent of the House would be required for this particular preamble. Obviously, there have been discussions.
I think it is helpful for the minister to have made the observations on the reasons for the preamble being expected and why it is being introduced in this way at this time. Therefore, it is helpful, in those terms, to know the reasons for it and the disposition of the House to support not only the idea of introducing the preamble but also the contents of the preamble as being acceptable in other ways. On the point of order I recognize the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Holmes)-

This, of course, was the critical issue throughout the debate and throughout the hearings conducted by the standing committee. I shall not spend time on any of the other problems which were experienced with regard to the James Bay bill; difficulties in terms of the adversary role by Quebec Hydro and other groups, the difficulties experienced by the Cree and the Inuit in terms of the province of Quebec and the government of Canada-the great difficulty they experienced in arriving at a final determination with respect to this agreement.
I want to focus on the critical issue of the so-called third parties or non-signatories to the agreement. What does this motion really talk about? We are talking about native individuals within the territory, or outside it, who may or may not have rights within the particular area involved in this agreement. It is my contention, and the contention on this side of the House, that if in fact rights do exist there has been gross injustice on the part of the government in extinguishing those
Janies Bay Agreement
rights unilaterally. If they do not exist, then obviously there is no problem. This has been the major contention throughout the entire standing committee hearings. That is the testimony we have heard from innumerable witnesses throughout the hearings.
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to go into detail at this time because I know hon. members will recognize that it is clause 2.3 of the bill before us, Bill C-9, and sections 2.14 and 2.16 of the agreement which must be related to this legislation. May I emphasize in this context that on a number of occasions we have given credit to the band council of the Cree, and specifically to Willie Diamond and to the Northern Quebec Inuit Association, for what they have accomplished under extremely difficult circumstances in arriving at a final agreement.
I wish to make it clear that the issue is with neither the band council of the Cree nor with the Northern Quebec Inuit Association who under very trying circumstances arrived at a final settlement-something they did under great adversity although they came up with some excellent sections within the agreement-but with the injustices contained in the legislation before us by which the government would unilaterally move to extinguish the rights of native people, individuals who have rights to that territory or who may well have such rights. The government would do this in unilateral fashion.
The injustice of the decision and of the legislation before us is implicit in the testimony which was given before the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
I have no intention of rehearsing that testimony, but I would simply say it would be a most important exercise for members of this House and, indeed, for people outside, to review the entire content of that evidence and realize what has transpired in terms of the difficulties the native groups experienced in arriving at a final agreement and in particular, the problems relating to the third parties or non-signatories who were completely ignored by the government.
When I spoke during second reading on December 7 last, I made reference to this important aspect and particularly to the Naskapi at Schefferville. It is my understanding that progress has been made with respect to negotiations in that particular area between the Naskapi and the government of Quebec and the government of Canada, and also with the Northern Quebec Inuit Association and the Cree. I would be interested to hear the minister tell us later in the debate precisely where those negotiations now stand, bearing in mind that when he appeared as a witness before the committee he told us in precise terms that he was interested in seeing an agreement consummated, and undertaking that when the legislation reached report stage in the House of Commons, if agreement had not been reached, or if members on this side of the House were not convinced that settlement of an agreement was imminent between the parties involved, he would delay third reading until a month had elapsed. I remind the minister of this because it is extremely important. It is one area in which we on this side of the House are hopeful that negotiations will be completed in terms of the Naskapi at Schefferville.

There is no question as to what is being done. I think the stakes are high for every native group which is involved. There is no question that the stakes are also very high for the governments and the Crown corporations and the other Indians who are involved. The idea is, in effect, to wipe the slate clean over a definite geographic area. There is no question that it is preferable that everybody and anybody who has any interest whatsoever in that full geographic area should be party to the agreement. That would have been the preference; that would have been the best thing. But that would have involved perhaps 20 or 25 groups.
That is the essence of the argument that we made. With Bill C-9 we took no objection to the Grand Council of the Cree or to the Northern Quebec Inuit Association changing some rights for other rights; but we do take exception to the fact that the group of natives who may have rights to that territory have those rights unilaterally extinguished and have no legal vehicle with which to appeal. The intention of the motion before us is to correct this situation. As I said, that was the substance of the debate during the standing committee hearings.
It was rather interesting that the issue of rights was discussed on many occasions. The legal counsel for the Grand Council of the Cree at that time indicated that it was difficult to understand these rights. So that is the dilemma with which Canada was faced. It is not a precedent that is a happy one. On the other hand, the other groups have been told for a couple of years actually that there is this problem, that this is happening, and they would prefer them to negotiate.

That testimony came out time and time again throughout the standing committee hearings. We have tried to make the case and we have tried repeatedly to emphasize that there has been gross injustice by this government unilaterally to exclude the rights of the third parties or non-signatories. There is nothing in that agreement which gives the Labrador people any reason for comfort. But there is a question of loyalty here, not to the Quebec government, not to the federal government, but to other Inuit and native people.
There is more than adequate testimony throughout their presentation indicating that the Labrador Inuit Association have grave concerns about this agreement. -there are three concerns, but the main one is this issue of consent or lack thereof of third parties to the agreement. That is the clause to which the motion now before the House refers.
-states quite clearly that the consents of the third parties will not be necessary to extinguish any native claims to the territory that they might have. In my view the minister has not addressed himself to that specific issue. He has not attempted to look for alternatives which would be viable for the Inuit communities as they evolve over a period of years. I would interpret them to be non-signatories, as third parties to the agreement, irrespective of the comments made at the standing committee hearings and irrespective of what comments the minister may make. I simply say that there has been no move by the government effectively to deal with this group.
On February 22 the Naskapi Indians of Schefferville appeared before the standing committee. I know the minister has concerned himself with this matter, and as I indicated earlier I hope he will tell us what progress has been made respecting this particular group, a group which, I may say, was initially ignored prior to the agreement in principle. It was only at the initiative of the opposition and other individuals that there was any movement on the part of the provincial government in the province of Quebec to involve themselves in resolving this issue. As I have said, I hope the minister will take the opportunity to bring the House up to date on what exactly has transpired, and tell us if his commitment holds in terms of his promise that there will not be a third reading until there has been at least some accommodation regarding that particular group, or there has been a settlement with the Naskapi of Schefferville.

On February 23, 1977, the Inuit Tapirisat of Canada made a strong presentation to the standing committee. Although they covered a number of aspects, one of the critically important issues referred to was the so-called third parties who were non-signatories to this agreement. I submit that all members of the House should read that testimony as well as the other testimony to which I alluded earlier.
I would also bring to the attention of the House the report by the Native Council of Canada and the Laurentian Alliance of Metis and Non-Status Indians who appeared before the standing committee on February 24, 1977. As I pointed out at the beginning of my remarks, the critical issue was, once again, the omission of third parties and non-signatories and their strong representation to the government to look at the matter carefully. They asked the government to reconsider and to bring in amendments which would satisfy the possible rights and needs of these individuals in the future. This is why this motion is before us today, to protect those third parties or non-signatories whose rights are to be extinguished by clause 3(3) of this bill.
On March 1, 1977, the standing committee received representations from Le Conseil Attikamek-Montagnais, a large delegation, and also from the Confederation of Indians of Quebec. I have no intention of going through the entire testimony, but once again, Mr. Speaker, numerous examples were given of possible rights as well as definite rights existing in the area and the unilateral action of extinguishing these rights without some means of protection, as exemplified by this motion before the House of Commons.
On Thursday, March 3, 1977, the Abitibi Dominion Band Council appeared before the standing committee and made a strong presentation in regard to the rights they had in the area which was being unilaterally extinguished. I have no intention of getting into the rather extensive legal arguments which took place throughout the standing committee hearings. I simply emphasize that the principal sections of the agreement, section 2.14 and 2.6, do not, in the opinion of legal counsel who appeared before the standing committee, indicate that there is any legal guarantee. Indeed, one of the senior officials of the Department of Justice appeared before one of the last meetings of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development, at which this question was asked of him:
If you were legal counsel for those third parties and non-signatories to the agreement, from your interpretation of the bill and of the agreement, what legal means have you at your disposal to protect the rights of those individuals which are being extinguished unilaterally?
His answer was very clear: he said that there was no legal right or commitment; there was only a moral commitment. Anyone who has studied the history of Indian affairs, the history of our native people in Canada, knows perfectly well that moral commitments are very empty in many instances. I have taken a good deal of the time of the House, Mr. Speaker, and I will have more to say on other aspects of the bill at third reading stage. I close on this key issue, which was the key issue throughout the entire debate on second reading and is the key issue at report stage. It is, without question, the grossest injustice that I have seen where the government in power can

James Bay Agreement
move unilaterally to extinguish the traditional rights of individuals in that area over a period of time. This amendment does nothing more than protect individuals who have rights or may have rights. As the motion indicates, we are simply saying that we would like paragraph 3.3 to include in the territory all Indians and all Inuit entitled to be enrolled as beneficiaries
under the agreement.
What could be more just than an amendment in that context? The Grand Council of Cree and the Northern Quebec Inuit Association have agreed to the agreement that is before us, together with the other signatories. What could be more just than for the government to say, "Yes, there has been an agreement. We will protect the rights of other individuals in the future, if they have rights, so that they will not be extinguished unilaterally"? That is the intention of the motion, that was the substance of the debate and our major concern during second reading, and again throughout the many hearings of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development.

I want to make it clear that the people living outside the territory who may have claims in the territory are not completely ignored or left out, as alleged by the hon. member. In fact, the agreement has opened the door to other native people in Quebec and elsewhere who are not entitled to benefit from its provisions but who may have claims in the territory. It

assures them of the chance to obtain certain rights and benefits which otherwise they might not have.
Under paragraph 2.14 of the agreement, Quebec has undertaken a legal obligation to negotiate with other Indians and Inuit concerning any claims they may be able to establish with respect to the territory. I think I should quote that part of the agreement. Paragraph 2.14 reads:
Quebec undertakes to negotiate with other Indians or Inuit who are not entitled to participate in the compensation and benefits of the present agreement, in respect to any claims which such Indians or Inuit may have with respect to the territory.
Questions were asked in the debate on second reading and the standing committee hearings with respect to these other groups not party to the agreement whose interests in the territory will be extinguished by Bill C-9. I would like to reiterate here that in the view of the federal government paragraph 2.14, which I just read, protects these non-signatory natives who can establish valid claims to the land and to the territory. This constitutes a legal obligation which the province has stated it fully intends to honour.
The hon. member said that when the chief counsel for the government appeared before the committee, he said this was only a moral obligation. That is not correct. As a matter of fact, there was considerable debate back and forth in the committee and counsel said-I do not have the proceedings with me, but I can bring them to the debate on third reading- that he considered paragraph 2.14, since it was part of a contract in effect, as a contractual obligation and as such was a legal obligation. I want to make clear, also, that in the inaugural address, or what is the new term for the speech from the throne in Quebec, before the National Assembly of Quebec on March 8, Premier Levesque confirmed his intention under the agreement in the following statement:

We will pursue our negotiations with other Indian nations to come to satisfying agreements with them.

So in the inaugural address, or speech from the throne given recently in Quebec, the government of Quebec said that it intended to honour its commitment under paragraph 2.14 of the agreement to negotiate with other groups of Indians who may not live in the territory but who might have claims there. Quebec's participation in the negotiations with the Naskapi of Schefferville, which are now nearing completion, is a concrete example of its willingness to negotiate pursuant to paragraph 2.14.

Probably the most interesting, challenging and informative exercise for hon. members to be involved in with the native peoples, particularly the native peoples of Quebec, came about as a result of the introduction of Bill C-9 and, of course, the James Bay agreement. As the hon. member for Lambton-Kent has said, the committee received delegations from a wide cross-section of native peoples. The hearings were very protracted. Indeed, on several occasions they were prolonged because testimony was given in the Inuit or Cree language and subsequently translated into the two official languages. Questions were addressed to the Cree and the Inuit, and they had to be translated into their native tongue.
If there was one thing that struck home throughout those hearings, it was the very true feeling these native peoples-the

April 28, 1977
James Bay Agreement
Cree, the Inuit, the Montagnais, the Naskapi and others- have for the land which they occupy, the land which they traditionally served long before the arrival of the white man. I think it was possible for some members to grasp for a moment the sense of living with nature-a communion with nature- which native peoples now rarely have the opportunity to experience, if they ever do, or if indeed they ever realize that that communion does exist.
One of the most interesting observations which could be made from those hearings was that in spite of the fact that the committee was dealing with Montagnais, Naskapi, Cree, Inuit and others, when it came to the fact that one band or another might be in what we would consider to be conflict over the same basic territorial rights, there was no conflict. Accommodations could be made whereby two or three different bands could agree to trap the same basic areas, to fish the same waters or to hunt the same territories. I think it is significant that the only time these native peoples expressed concern about the loss of their traditional rights was when non-native peoples became actively involved with the utilization or overutilization of their traditional areas.
Relatively few people have had the opportunity to fly over the areas of northern Quebec which are occupied by these people, particularly the Cree. When landing on a remote river or on a small, remote lake, it is interesting to find that they are not really remote, that the shore selected for a campground has for centuries served as a campground, and that the trail selected is a trail which has for centuries been shared by animals and by the Cree.
The members of the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry who directed their attention to the leghold trap and the whole question of trapping learned much from listening to the Cree who for centuries have been trappers and have lived off the land. Throughout the hearings of the standing committee on Bill C-9 committee members consistently heard expressions of concern for the rights of third party signatories, and I find it difficult to understand why government members of the committee did not seem to heed such concerns. They had no conception of the problem. I suggest they were not as sympathetic as we were to the concerns of third party signatories. Or, if they perceived the problem at hand and were concerned, they did not appear to address their attention to such matters.
I find that most unfortunate because it was a reflection on the ministry and a reflection on how the government, not parliament, views the concerns of Canada's native peoples. For that reason alone I was more than surprised to note that some government members on the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development were not as concerned as we were about the questions before the committee.
The minister has suggested that an option is open for the non-signatories, that is, for the third parties. He has suggested that Quebec entered into an agreement whereby the people concerned may negotiate claims to territories outlined in the agreement, territories in which they as Indian or Inuit people

may have an interest. The operative words are "in which they may have some interest." I find the use of the word "may ominous for it puts the whole issue in doubt.
I am surprised to note that the government has failed to convince the new government of Quebec to implement the sort of provisions which would flow from acceptance of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent. I wonder how effectively the minister addressed himself to that issue, or how assiduously the ministry worked on this question.
I find it difficult to understand why the federal government has not been able to resolve this issue, why it did not discuss with the former Liberal government of Quebec questions of genuine concern relating to the extinction of native rights. I find it strange that this has not happened. I do not find it strange that the government may have some difficulty in this respect at present. However, I am surprised that there has not been a greater measure of response with regard to these questions from those now charged with the control of the affairs of Quebec and, indeed, perhaps the destiny of this country.
The question arose in the committee hearings as to how effective is the moccasin telegraph. It became clear that third party individuals, third party non-signatories who frequently testified before the committee, did not know whom to approach, to whom they should talk, if they should approach the department or if the department was supposed to approach them. Some of the native peoples in Canada have developed a certain expertise in approaching the government. But that expertise is not available to people like the Montagnais who live in the mountains and hills of Labrador, far removed from contact with non-natives and whites.
To our great interest we learned from one of the first groups to appear before us-they were native people from the northern part of Quebec-that when they first traded with the white man it was not with the federal government and not with the government of the province of Quebec. Their first contact with the white man was with the Hudson's Bay Company. Their conception of the Hudson's Bay Company was interesting. Of course, it was in the best interests of that company of northwestern adventurers to provide for the needs of the native peoples. Whether it was in the company's best interest or not, the fact remains that it accepted a degree of responsibility for the Inuit people which had never been demonstrated by the federal government.
Widows and children were given food and clothing by the company and provided with regular rations. The company allowed nobody to starve, and nobody was turned away. This exercise cost the Hudson's Bay Company a great deal of money. It was suggested that perhaps we ought to operate under some kind of sharing commitment. Really, I am relating the story to you, Mr. Speaker, just as it was related to the standing committee.
The Hudson's Bay Company approached the federal government and said, "Although we do not mind fulfilling this particular responsibility, we would appreciate a little help." But the federal government, in its wisdom and charity, said,
April 28, 1977

"No, do it yourself." Hoping for a more positive response from the province of Quebec, the Hudson's Bay Company approached that provincial government and made the same request. The province of Quebec, again demonstrating its idea of charity, said "No." The Hudson's Bay Company was forced to carry the can. Eventually the federal government and the provincial government agreed to accept responsibility in this regard.
Let me note one thing for the record. I want to mention the work of a man who has lately changed the political climate of this country a great deal. I am not one of his supporters. Let me tell the House who told tjie Inuit and native people of the province of Quebec, the people who live along James Bay, Ungava Bay, Hudson Bay and the eastern Arctic that they were citizens of the province of Quebec. They first learned in the 1950s they were citizens of the province when a certain gentleman travelled through their communities and told them so. Mr. Speaker, interestingly enough, the man who told them was none other than Rene Levesque.
I would say he probably demonstrated at that time a greater measure of understanding for the native peoples than he appears to be demonstrating today by refusing to negotiate this one basic clause that provides for some traditional democracy. Does no one think it strange that in 1977-not 1877 or 1795-in this so-called enlightened era of Canadian democracy that we are listening to a government fully prepared to move ahead in this fashion with our native peoples, when at this very time the native peoples of the Yukon and the Northwest Territories are concerned about their traditional native rights?
I wonder how this action of the government is going to affect their thinking and their actions at the bargaining table. What kind of a bargain do they hope to strike? To me and, I am sure, to many Canadians, the word "extinguishment" is abhorrent. I would have thought that even though "a rose by any other name", this government would have demonstrated a greater sense of responsibility and sensitivity and would have used another word that was not as damning and final.
I want it clearly on the record that, without equivocation, I fully support motion No. 2 presented today by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent.
