subsubtopic: COMMUNICATIONS RESPECTING 200-MILE FISHERIES ZONE
speechtext:
That an humble address be presented to His Excellency praying that he will cause to be laid before this House copies of all documents, minutes of meetings, telegrams, etc., relating to the discussions between the government and the governments of the United States, France and Denmark with regard to the proposed 200-mile limit.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on motion No. 47 which asks that copies of all documents, minutes of meetings, telegrams, etc., relating to the discussions between the government and the government of the United States, France and Denmark with regard to the proposed 200-mile limit be laid before this House.
At the present time there is much concern in the minds of Canadian inshore and offshore fishermen, as well as Canadian plant owners and shore workers, over what the future holds for them in the fishing industry. This concern is, of course, justified because decisions are being made on their behalf by so-called unknown experts at Ottawa without benefit of discussion, consultation or debate in the House of Commons on matters which will have a direct bearing on the future of thousands of Canadians in Atlantic Canada and on the west coast.
We have been told, for example, in response to questions which I put to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson), that discussions have been held with American officials, with French and Danish officials over fishing rights and quotas and mineral rights in the disputed areas such as Georges Bank off Nova Scotia, the fishing grounds around St. Pierre and Miquelon, the French fishing rights in the Gulf of St. Lawrence, and fishing rights as they exist in the Davis Strait between Greenland and Canada.
I understand that Alan Beesley of the Department of External Affairs has said that negotiations with the United States on Georges Bank have been at a standstill. It has been seven months-from last September-since Canadian and American negotiators met to discuss boundaries. No further meetings have been held, which causes me to ask: What is the problem? On an issue of such crucial importance to the Canadian fishery, one has to ask: Why have there been such lengthy delays? No wonder there has not been any progress in settling the various boundary disputes with the United States.
Our fisheries negotiators have only been able to work out an interim agreement with the United States. Interim agreements are often less than satisfactory because no long-range planning can be done with any confidence. Our Fisheries negotiators are ready to begin talks with their American counterparts on a long-term fishing agreement, but so far they have only been standing by, waiting for a boundary agreement to be reached.
It should be noted that the interim agreement which was reached and was triumphantly announced by this government
80012-44>/2

April 28, 1977
Fisheries
has not as yet been ratified by the United States Congress. It has been bogged down in the United States Senate, although hearings will soon begin. Since we are not as yet assured that this interim agreement will be enacted, I would call the government's announcement a very hollow triumph. I submit that the Canadian people, especially those involved in the fishing industry, have a right to know what is being discussed. They have a right to know what the bones of contention are and what is being bartered away by our so-called government experts behind closed doors.
Our people in Atlantic Canada are not only concerned about the outcome of the discussions between the Canadian government and the three countries which are the subject of this motion. They are also vitally concerned over the manner in which this government proposes to manage the fishery resources within the 200-mile limit unilaterally declared on January 1, 1977.
Our chief negotiator at the law of the sea conference, Mr. Beesley, told me that for 1977 the system used by ICNAF, the International Commission for North Atlantic Fisheries, has now been integrated into our domestic management process. In light of ICNAF's failure over the years properly to manage our fish stocks, some of which have been fished below the sustainable yield level, Mr. Beesley's statement raises more questions in my mind than answers. I can appreciate what our negotiators are trying to accomplish at the law of the sea conference, but I ask: What are the tangible benefits for the fishermen of Atlantic Canada? Is it not true that our inshore and offshore fishermen are now on the short end of the stick because of Canada's conciliatory approach at the law of the sea conference and in the more specific application of its principles by the so-called fishery management experts in Ottawa?
I still have grave doubts about the importance which the Trudeau government attaches to the east coast fisheries, and even graver doubts about its ability to measure the importance of our fishery when considering all of the so-called national interests to be dealt with by the law of the sea conference. During the past year two new factors have complicated discussions about the 200-mile limit and its importance to our fisheries, namely, bilateral fishing agreements and joint ventures. Canada was very polite and diplomatic when she declared her 200-mile zone unilaterally. In order to make the limit more acceptable to foreign fishing fleets, she decided to make certain concessions called bilateral fishing agreements.
These concessions were made separately between Canada and each of the foreign fishing nations formerly fishing in our waters. They were concessions which were never discussed and approved by our Canadian fishermen or their representatives in their various fishing associations. These concessions give countries like Poland, Russia or West Germany the right to harvest surplus fish stocks. In other words, Canada decides what total allowable catches should be, figures out what our harvesting capacity is and then gives away the difference.
The bilateral agreements do not specify the exact amount of fish we will concede. The unwritten understanding is that the

Russians, the Poles, the Cubans, the West Germans, the Portuguese and the Spanish will get enough to keep them happy. However, our inshore and our offshore fishermen are asking: Where is this resource surplus everyone is talking about, especially government supporters? In answer to this question, fishery experts offer some complex biological information, but in words that everyone can understand there is no oversupply but there is a critical shortage. To most of us, including the average fisherman, the word "surplus" suggests an overabundance or an excess supply of fish. It implies that there is enough fish to go around for every man or every woman to make a decent living, with some left over. The most important meaning of "surplus" relates to its application in the management of our new 200-mile limit.
Article 50 of the draft law of the sea which Canada is now using to manage her 200-mile economic zone broadly defines "surplus" as the difference between the estimated total allowable catch, or TAC which is used for short, and Canada's ability to catch that amount of fish. The catching capacity for Canada is the quantity of fish she can catch using all vessels, inshore as well as offshore.
This brings to my mind a formula which goes something like this: total allowable catch, minus Canada's catching capacity, equals what our government experts call "surplus". The surplus defined by this formula must be given, under the law of the sea principles, to any foreign nation operating in Canada's coastal waters. However, Canada can still impose certain terms and conditions as to the method used to harvest this surplus. The real secret of this equation lies not in the definition of surplus but, rather, in how we calculate the TAC, or the total allowable catch.
The way this figure is calculated has important implications for our east coast fishermen. This calls for an equation which starts with maximum sustainable yield, minus stock replenishment factor, minus inshore community factor, which equals the total allowable catch.
The maximum sustainable yield is the quantity of fish caught which will allow the stock to reproduce itself naturally. The stock replenishment factor is a quantity of fish which is set aside to allow the stock to rebuild itself more rapidly. This is only a temporary measure because in the past stocks may have been overfished. The inshore community factor is a quantity of fish set aside to protect the social and economic viability of coastal fishing communities. This last factor is perhaps the most important. If we do not understand what it implies, then we cannot create a development policy for our inshore fishermen.
Article 50(3) of the law of the sea proposals allows Canada to set aside a certain quantity of fish which will provide for the maintenance and development of an inshore fishery. It grants us the right to take special care that fishing effort offshore does not destroy the economic base of inshore communities which depend upon the same resource for survival. Unfortu-
April 28, 1977

nately, 1977 has become a year of transition; it has also become a year of confusion.
Since 1973 the International Commission for the North Atlantic Fishery, ICNAF, has been setting limits for quotas on the amount of fish caught in the northwest Atlantic. This came about because these waters had been overfished or overexploited during the preceding 10 or 12 years. But essentially the ICNAF quotas have been set through a process of back-scratching, or horse-trading, an international political exercise which has meant quotas have been set too high. This happened because the quotas were set on the basis of historical catch records and not on scientific, biological information.
For example, Mr. Speaker, the Russians, to name but one nation, have been catching a tremendous amount of fish each year since the late 1950s. At the yearly ICNAF meetings they have therefore argued that the next year's quota should be based on their previous performance, without any regard for its effects on the total fish stocks in our waters. In other words, the word "surplus" now takes on a new meaning which, under present fisheries management plans, means the "allowable foreign catch", which is not good enough to satisfy the needs of Canadian fishermen.
Joint ventures are yet another kettle of fish in the present mess. These arrangements, made so far only with West Germany, do not relate to the surplus I have been describing but, rather, relate to an uncaught portion of the Canadian quota. For example, in 1976 the Canadian offshore cod quota on the Hamilton Bank was about 20,000 metric tons. However, our draggers only managed to catch about 3,000 metric tons. This year the province of Newfoundland arranged for West German boats to catch some 6,000 tons of the 1977 Canadian offshore quota and to land the fish in Newfoundland ports, an arrangement which will create some jobs within the provincial processing industry. However, both bilateral agreements and joint venture arrangements merely complicate an already confused fisheries development policy.
I say this, Mr. Speaker, because shortly after the joint venture system was announced it began to develop its own set of complications. Here I refer to the fact that processors and fishing interests in my native province of Nova Scotia wanted to establish their own joint venture plan with West German interests, but this request was denied. All of these moves and countermoves have reduced our ability to consider more simple, short-term solutions to the present resource problem.
Looking ahead to 1978, we have the power to make small changes, but they are changes that will bring significant benefits to our fishermen. The 200-mile limit presents us in Atlantic Canada with a golden opportunity, but we have a tendency to look ahead with a 10-year vision and not to look with vision to the immediate needs of our people, to their needs this month, next month and throughout 1977. In any case,
1976	ICNAF quota negotiations did not set a limit on the
1977	inshore quota. Instead, they estimated that the inshore catch would be around 50,000 metric tons. However, the actual catch in 1976 was 53,000 metric tons. If a number of conditions are right this summer, the inshore catch, for exam-
Fisheries
pie, in ICNAF zones 2J and 3KL could go as high as 75,000 to 80,000 tons.
I submit that the federal government would not take any action to prevent inshore Fishermen from fishing beyond their estimated 50,000 tons, for to do so would be political suicide. This combination of factors could make the 1977 inshore cod fishery the most exciting in years. Nobody planned it as such, but now the inshore fleet has an opportunity to demonstrate its efficiency and the desirability of having a higher stock level at the end of the spring offshore fishery.
If the 1977 fishery becomes a success, what short-term measures can we take to ensure an even better one for 1978? In my opinion, the problem at present is that discussions on the 1978 quotas are taking place at this very moment while I am speaking in the House. These meetings could well decide the fate of the 1978 fishery before important information is available about the 1977 inshore catch. In other words, the danger exists that once again in 1978 there will be a surplus declared on the Hamilton Bank cod stocks, and consequently foreign fleets will once more have a right to harvest these fish. I submit that that would be a disaster for our Canadian Fishermen.
The most important fisheries problem facing this government at present is the question of the 1978 quotas. Quotas for our inshore fishermen, and especially those on the northeast and Labrador coasts, should not be allocated at least until September when some of the effect of this year's effort is known. If the inshore catch increases, the government could quite correctly increase 1978's inshore fishing quota, and by doing so further reduce foreign offshore fishing on the offshore banks, especially on Hamilton Bank. This will mean increased earnings for Canadians and increased social benefits in our fishing communities.
We in Canada seem reluctant to make relatively simple decisions because the whole policy-making process within the fisheries department is carried out in secrecy. Next to the budget, proposed quotas are the best kept secret in government. There has never been any public debate on this issue. Nor has any significant amount of information been made available by government, which is the reason for this motion today. Consequently, we go on pretending that this complex task is rightly the business of a host of experts in Ottawa.
Meanwhile, the United States encourages public participation in setting quotas through its regional advisory councils, and even gives these groups the right to veto quotas which are set by experts. I ask, why cannot we do the same thing in Canada? Decisions about quotas, limits and fisheries development should become a matter of public debate, in my opinion, in Atlantic Canada, with input from fishermen, from the trade and from the general public affected by the rulings made by these mystery men in Ottawa.
A major focus in this debate should be on the balance between inshore and offshore effort, and on which development strategy provides the maximum social and economic benefits to those associated with the fisheries in Atlantic Canada. We should openly discuss these issues and not merely

April 28, 1977
Fisheries
turn them over to a battery of so-called experts in Ottawa for further study. The trouble with this government-perhaps I should say, one of the many troubles with this government-is that they automatically reject the idea of participation in policy-making. Perhaps the problem of a simple reappraisal of our inshore and offshore harvesting capacity is not expensive, exciting or large-scale enough to satisfy government planners. In the words of one fisherman who spoke to me about it, "Lloyd, let's face it; the fishing industry and its problems really don't have much sex appeal". Perhaps that describes the situation generally in the terminology of today. I submit that this action is necessary if our fisheries management policy is to be effective and if it is to bring long-term economic and social benefits to the majority of our people.
All I am asking is that this government lift the veil of secrecy with which it presently cloaks its activities. Let the light of discussion and consultation replace the darkness of secrecy and confrontation. Denial of my request for information will once again show the need for an effective freedom of information act. The public, especially members of the House, have a right to know what the government is doing and how it is doing it. As the cloak of secrecy which the government throws around its operations grows, so does public mistrust of this government. I find that mistrust of this government by the Canadian people is at an all-time high. I submit that this trend must be reversed, for the benefit of Canada. The releasing of documents which I have requested in this motion today would be a step in the right direction.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Fleming (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subsubtopic: COMMUNICATIONS RESPECTING 200-MILE FISHERIES ZONE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question which has been asked in the House regarding communications and discussions between Canada and other countries in connection with the 200-mile fishing limit deserves some comment. It also deserves a review concerning the role these communications and discussions have played in the process of extending our jurisdiction. I would like to deal with that in the knowledge that my colleague, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Leblanc) will be dealing particularly with the problems of producing these papers later this day.
The 200-mile fishing zone established by Canada on January 1, 1977, represents one of the outstanding achievements of Canadian diplomacy and is the fruit of years of effort. The very success of this operation, however, may obscure both its importance and the difficulties that had to be overcome along the way. In this quiet and orderly assumption of management authority over 630,000 square miles of high seas, Canada has set a model for the world and especially for other coastal states. Canada has done more than perhaps any other country to transform the 200-mile limit from a highly controversial, hotly disputed proposition favoured by a small minority of states to an established fact of life and law accepted by all, whether explicitly or implicitly.

The accomplishment is all the more remarkable in that Canada had one of the greatest concentrations of foreign fishing fleets in the world off its coasts, operated in some cases by the most powerful countries in the world, and in all cases by countries determined to resist any take-over of the high seas and any encroachment on the freedom of fishing recognized by international law for so many centuries. To achieve this objective Canada has had to take many initiatives in terms of our multilateral and bilateral international relations.
Multilaterally, Canada was one of the handful of countries chiefly responsible for bringing about a consensus on the 200-mile fisheries limit at the UN law of the sea conference which has helped to transform customary international law and to make it possible for countries like Canada to adopt the 200-mile limit without provoking chaos or conflict. One of the most basic elements of this consensus is the principle of optimum utilization which simply means that coastal states will not allow fish stocks under their jurisdiction to die of old age and go to waste but, rather, will allow other countries access to such portions of the stocks as may be surplus to the coastal state's harvesting capacity as determined by the coastal state. This has proved to be the keystone in the process of achieving international acceptance of the 200-mile fishing limit.
While working to advance Canadian fisheries interests at the law of the sea conference, Canada was also pursuing regional initiatives to this same end, in particular through the International Commission for the Northwest Atlantic Fisheries-ICNAF. Beginning in 1972 we obtained in ICNAF steadily growing recognition of the coastal state's preferential rights in the harvest of fishery resources off its shores. In 1975 we obtained in ICNAF, for 1976, a 40 per cent reduction in foreign fishing effort for groundfish, as well as a reduction in the total allowable catches-TACs-for depleted stocks, and higher quotas for Canadian fishermen on stocks of particular importance to them. In 1976 we obtained in ICNAF, for 1977, the further reduction in TACs we considered necessary, together with estimated allocation in TACs we considered necessary, together with estimated allocations for Canadian fishermen generally corresponding to their harvesting capacity. In effect, this amounted to recognition of extended Canadian fisheries jurisdiction even before that extension had taken place.
Nor is this all. In the closing weeks of 1976 Canada achieved another historic first by securing agreement on amendments to the ICNAF convention that restrict the commission's management authority to the area beyond national fisheries limits and leaves management within 200 miles to the authority of the coastal state, while also leaving Canada with the right to board and inspect foreign vessels beyond the 200-mile limit under the ICNAF scheme of joint international enforcement.
No other international commission has yet adapted itself in this way to extended fisheries jurisdiction, although at least one other is beginning to follow suit, using the Canadian approach as both model and precedent. Together with these
April 28, 1977

Canadian amendments, ICNAF also adopted a Canadian-sponsored resolution calling for the establishment of new arrangements for multilateral co-operation with regard to the northwest Atlantic fisheries, in keeping with the new jurisdictional realities. A preparatory conference has been held in Ottawa to prepare for a diplomatic conference for this purpose in 1977. It is imperative that we work out such arrangements for the protection of important Canadian fisheries in the area immediately beyond the 200-mile limit.
The multilateral and regional initiatives which I have noted were also complemented by a series of bilateral initiatives. In 1975 we began negotiations with five countries responsible for some 90 per cent of the foreign catch off our coasts-Norway, Poland, the U.S.S.R., Portugal and Spain. In less than a year we had concluded bilateral agreements with all of them. More recently we also worked out a practical arrangement with Japan, for 1977, having much the same effect as the formal agreements in terms of control and licensing.
These bilateral agreements were the first ever to anticipate extension of fisheries jurisdiction by a coastal state and to be based on the consensus reached at the law of the sea conference, including the consensus on optimum utilization. As early as 1972 Canada had also incorporated certain provisions in anticipation of extension of jurisdiction in a bilateral agreement with France. The agreement with the U.S.S.R. was the first in which that country undertook to recognize and comply with a coastal state's jurisdiction in the 200-mile zone. It is surely a unique tribute to these Canadian agreements that they have been widely used as models in bilateral negotiations by other countries, both coastal states and distant-water fishing states.
To bring the picture up to date, I would add that on February 24, 1977, a reciprocal fisheries agreement was negotiated with the U.S.A. to provide for the continuation of existing fisheries by fishermen of each country off the coast of the other while we proceed with negotiations aimed at establishing boundaries between the fishing zones of the two countries and long-term reciprocal fishing relations.
Canada's approach to extended jurisdiction was the right one and the practical one, for a number of reasons. We have other vital objectives yet to secure at the law of the sea conference in the field of fisheries and in other fields as well. We have, for example, negotiated a draft provision for the proposed new law of the sea convention that would assure the protection of salmon of Canadian origin during those periods when they migrate outside our 200-mile zone. We have negotiated a draft provision recognizing our sovereign rights over continental shelf resources beyond 200 miles to the outer edge of the continental margin. We have negotiated a draft provision recognizing our right to impose the most stringent rules and standards for the prevention of pollution from ships in our Arctic waters. Our process of consultation and discussion with other countries to achieve our fisheries objectives has avoided jeopardizing these achievements as we move closer to a new law of the sea convention.
There is still another important reason why Canada's approach has been the appropriate one. The 200-mile limit on
Fisheries
the Atlantic coast does not enclose all of our continental shelf fish stocks but leaves some 10 per cent of them outside our jurisdiction, including some stocks of particular importance to Canadian fishermen. It is, accordingly, essential that we have the co-operation of other countries to ensure the proper conservation and management of these outside stocks and appropriate allocations for Canadian fishermen. Our approach to extended jurisdiction has secured us that co-operation so far. As I have already indicated, we will now be seeking to ensure such co-operation in future through the negotiation of a new convention to replace ICNAF. Among the most important tasks yet to be completed are marine boundary negotiations to be pursued with Denmark, France and the United States.
Mr. Speaker, I have reviewed in some detail our international relations over the last few years in connection with the extension of Canadian fisheries jurisdiction to 200 miles.
Though the question which gave rise to this review related only to the U.S.A., France and Denmark, it is important to note that discussions and communications with all three have spanned the areas I have reviewed: our multinational, regional, and bilateral involvements. Though the discussions and communications cannot be made public, for obvious reasons which will be pointed out in a few moments by my colleague, I have recounted for the House the story they tell, apart from the question of boundary negotiations which are still in process.

subsubtopic: COMMUNICATIONS RESPECTING 200-MILE FISHERIES ZONE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while in an elementary way the remarks of the previous speaker are quite correct, in an historical way all the moves which have been described are those which have been taken to correct a wrong which resulted from a lack of knowledge, and from a very poor planning structure as it related to government planning for fishing. To some degree all of the conflict in respect of how much fish should be caught and how much fish could be caught, initially arose from a statement made by an official of the Department of Fisheries which indicated-this was approximately ten years ago or perhaps a little more- that the amount of herring, for instance, in the Atlantic Ocean was beyond the catching capability of anybody, including the Russians, and therefore that there should be an open fishing policy for herring in the Atlantic Ocean. This really resulted in an infusion of new catching capability from foreign countries which had never before been present in this fishing operation.
It was not because of good planning that we have now exercised control of the 200 mile limit; it was because of shortsightedness and poor planning, and any credit which the government may wish to cuddle to its arms today as a result of those efforts to correct its errors of the past certainly is of minimal importance to the fishermen who can no longer depend upon the sea as a source of proper livelihood as they could in days gone by. So let there be no confusion as to why we have a 200 mile limit. It was clearly lack of knowledge and lack of attachment of importance to the fishing industry which put us in the position whereby the Government of Canada had no choice, if it was to have a fishing industry at all, but to coax

April 28, 1977
Fisheries
and persuade the world fishing nations that we must have a 200 mile limit and that we must now, after a period of profligate fishing at the expense of the population in the sea, have a return to a rational approach to the fishing industry.
Things were further complicated by the fact that when there were obvious marketing problems for the products of the sea, there was no impetus put into the sale of the product by the government. Instead, others expanded their fleets, improved their techniques and caught the fish while we stood idly by, until even with the capabilities we had ten years ago we no longer had an adequate stock to support either the fishing fleet or the processing industry ashore. Of course there is no question but that it is possible for a stock to get over age and to get too large in numbers and therefore, as nature sometimes balances itself in our ecological structure, there is a waste of that stock.
I noticed that when the hon. member spoke about salmon he avoided mentioning Atlantic salmon, and unless I am in error there is no protection for salmon as they leave the Atlantic coast and go beyond the 200 mile limit. This is something which has been reserved for the west coast. I would not object to an interruption if I am inaccurate, but that is my understanding of the situation as it is at the moment. I think this is an item of shameful neglect. We should attend to the salmon on both coasts of Canada, not on just one coast.
I do not believe the previous speaker had any conception of the importance of salmon fishing to local communities both on the coast and along the streams in the provinces which are favoured by the presence of Atlantic salmon. This supply has been robbed and decimated by overfishing at sea well beyond the 200 mile limit, and we still exercise little, if any control. Granted, there has been an element of negotiation in that regard, but there has been no confirmation to date-at least which the minister announced-that these salmon are now protected and that they are in fact available to the Atlantic fishery for commmercial or for sport purposes.
The problem with secrecy in the negotiations is a major one, and the request for information is an important one. I submit that it should be accepted as a necessity for future planning at both the processing and fishing levels. The guidelines which these agreements have set down are going to be the guidelines for any new purchase of equipment, for any expansion of plant, for any disposal of equipment, or for any disposal of plant. In other words this is the economic base which has now been negotiated for the industry both on the water and on the land. I submit that if this information is denied it will be a great disservice to every aspect of the fishing industry, as it tries to generate a livelihood for industries both afloat and ashore. This information is a must. The industry is now fishing and processing in ignorance of what is its long-term future. There has been virtually no open participation in respect of what the government will negotiate with regard to fisheries.
True, in the past there has been an element of consultation. The Fisheries Council has been consulted. Some fisheries organizations have been consulted. One fisherman told me that he actually went on a trip to a negotiating meeting, that he

was given a little bit of information, that a few documents were passed to him for his consideration, but that before he had time to read them they were removed from his hands. They were then put into a virtual lock-up until after the negotiations had taken place. In the meantime this fisherman had no opportunity to make constructive suggestions as to what would be in the best interests of the fishing industry. There is no meaningful consultation. I think it is imperative that this be restored. Since that fisherman was not consulted, he should at least be informed of the consequences of the negotiation in which he was unable to play any part whatsoever.
One of the problems at the present time-and again this is why we need to see this information-is that the Canadian research capability has never at any time been able to state authoritatively that there are so many tons of fish to be caught, so many haddock, halibut, cod, herring, lobsters or any other variety. It has been admitted, frankly and openly, that as far as statistics are concerned in deciding what should be the catch, they have been supplied piecemeal by various other nations which have been fishing on the spot.
We have not had a capability to determine accurately what tonnage of what species can be removed from the sea without a depletion of the stock. This is negligence of the worst kind. Since we did not have personal knowledge of what those stocks were, how could we wisely negotiate with anybody in the past as to what we should give away and what should be the allowable catch for this or any other nation? I submit that while we must trust our fellowmen and our neighbours, there is an inclination by anybody to submit statistics which would favour himself and which would increase the catch he would like to have.
What is a surplus? Is a surplus the amount we catch in one year or the amount we do not catch in one year? I submit that the answer is no. For instance, in the seining fleet in the herring industry there was a catch capability which was never properly satisfied since the imposition of quotas, and yet we negotiated the quota downward until we had to allocate individual boat quotas, and while this improved the situation for the seiner, it certainly did not exercise his capability to catch.
Having estimated capability too late, we have traded away that which we ought to have retained and we have not recovered for our own consumption anything like the stocks of fish we are capable of catching. We must therefore develop a highly sophisticated research program to enable us to estimate exactly what is in the sea. Only then can we estimate what we should allow others to catch in total, and what our fishermen should catch. We should give away only that amount which is beyond our capability to catch. The total allowable catch with regard to any species can only be considered after we have estimated what we can process and catch for ourselves.
If we are to determine quota levels by September, we must consult with fishing groups. They are on the sea and have a
April 28, 1977

pretty good idea of the size of various stocks of fish. No, they cannot tell you how many tons are out there, but they can give you a pretty good idea, a better idea I suggest than some researchers. Only by consulting such groups can we set catch levels. For instance, we must know if we are catching too many fish. Is the fish population up, or is it down? If it is down, what can we do to bring it up again? I suggest that researchers in the field of fishing rely on fishermen to confirm their findings.
My second point is that, not only must we consult participants in fishing, we must also make certain that an adequate research capability is in place. We must invite those who catch and process all kinds of fish, that is to say, people in all parts of the fishing industry, to help us in the determination of the present size of fish populations. We must know if we are depleting fish stocks. Let us consult all concerned, and let us not rely on a single source of information. That one cannot rely on a single source of information has been demonstrated to farmers who have relied on figures supplied by one source of statistics with regard to farm product stocks on hand. I suggest that it is even more difficult to estimate what is in the sea. Let us therefore use our research capabilities and the knowledge of our fishermen to determine how large are our fish stocks in the sea.
Let us put our fishermen back in business so that we may remove some of the subsidies we have been forced to put in place. We were forced to pay subsidies because fishermen were not allowed to catch enough. Let us put all these things on the table. Let those both afloat and ashore share in the making of these plans. This is imperative. Let us make sure that our trade structure is working in the markets of the world, so that we can sell in those markets those products we are capable of producing and preparing.

speakeroldname: Mr. Fernand E. Leblanc (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: COMMUNICATIONS RESPECTING 200-MILE FISHERIES ZONE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I see we are discussing the notice of motion for papers and the three previous speakers have dealt at length with the substance of the motion, namely the 200-mile zone and fisheries. Mr. Speaker, concerning Standing Order 48(2), I think we should rather deal with the fact that for some reason or another, which I shall explain later, the government is unable to table the documents requested by the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse), and in my opinion it is more precisely the tabling of documents which is the subject of the motion.
So, Mr. Speaker, I shall rather restrict myself to the history of the freedom of information which was instituted by the present government many years ago. We must remember, Mr. Speaker, that before 1973, there was no rule forcing the government to table documents, and that the decision remained with the minister or the Crown corporations from whom documents were requested.
But in 1973, a motion concerning the production of papers was passed in the House of Commons. 1 think it is a good thing to remind hon. members that in those guidelines for production of papers, there was in appendix "B" of Hansard for March 15, 1973 a notice of motion for the production of
Fisheries
papers and the general principle established at that time was the following, and I quote:
To enable Members of Parliament to secure factual information about the operations of government to carry out their parliamentary duties and to make public as much factual information as possible consistant with effective administration, the protection of the security of the state, righs to privacy and other such matters, government papers, documents and consultant reports should be produced on Notice of Motion for the Production of Papers unless falling within the categories outlined below in which case an exemption is to be claimed from production.
There are 16 specific exemptions concerning ministers' correspondence and of course consultant studies.
I note that the third exemption which was accepted by all the members of the House at that time reads as follows, and 1 quote:
3. Papers dealing with international relations, the release of which might be detrimental to the future conduct of Canada's foreign relations; (the release of papers received from other countries to be subject to the consent of the originating country).
So I think that the motion of the hon. member for South Shore for the production of copies of documents, minutes of meetings, telegrams and others regarding discussions between the federal government and the United States, France and Denmark in connection with the proposed 200-mile fishing zone, fall specifically under exemption No. 3 since, as an hon. member stated before me, negotiations are not yet completed. Indeed the release of these documents could have a detrimental effect on the maintenance of good relations between Canada and foreign countries. Also, cabinet documents and those which include a Privy Council confidence are exempt under exemption No. 12. A number of documents which the hon. member for South Shore referred to fall under exemption No. 12; exemption No. 16 reads, and I quote:
Papers requested, submitted or received in confidence by the government from sources outside the government.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we cannot release these documents, telegrams and other papers which are still used in negotiations, because we have not received permission from the foreign countries involved to release them. Moreover, the release of these documents could prove detrimental to the negotiations being carried out.
Mr. Speaker, since the issuing of the guidelines which were tabled in the House in March 1973 and which I have just mentioned, the government, being well aware of the problem and anxious to make government papers available to the Canadian people as a whole, and to hon. members in particular, referred the bill of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) which relates to the publication of these documents to the Joint Standing Committee on Regulations and other Statutory Instruments, and the whole substance of the problem was also referred on this occasion. I had the honour and the pleasure to sit on this committee for a few years, and we had about 25 sittings in which we discussed the possibility of making more documents available to the public and to hon. members; we even went to Washington to study the methods established in the United States for the production of documents.

April 28, 1977
Fisheries
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, in the Speech from the Throne of October 12, 1976, it is mentioned that the government is well aware of the problems and wishes to make public as many documents as possible. I shall quote from Part III which relates to individual rights and which is of particular interest to us this evening. We can read this in the Speech from the Throne, and I quote:
At a time of growing complexity in public affairs it is especially important to enhance the citizen's right of access to the information necessary to make well-informed judgments and take responsible action.
The Government therefore places great value on the continuing work of the joint parliamentary committee which has been studying the question of freedom of information, and plans to submit a policy paper to that committee in the hope that early agreement might be reached on the best methods to improve public access to government information. In the meantime, the Government will increase the number and range of internal documents available to the public.
That is what we have done, and especially we in the Department of External Affairs of course want to publish as many documents as possible, and we feel that the issue raised by the hon. member for South Shore is very important since it challenges the principle behind document production.
At present-
-the government will be pleased to table the arbitration award of 1903 and the treaty of 1904 between Great Britain and the United States ratifying that award. The government is also prepared to table the orders in council relating to Canadian jurisdiction over the waters inside Dixon Entrance.
We shall be pleased to table the treaty of 1825 between Great Britain and Russia, and the treaty of 1867 between Imperial Russia and the United States.

There are some, Mr. Speaker, who seem to find strange that I refer to documents published so long ago, but all those documents now bring us back to the negotiations in question about the 200-mile limit and that is why we think those documents could be important if hon. members wanted us to lay them down. Of course, we would be prepared to do so. [English]
We will be pleased to table the 1958 Geneva Convention on the Continental Shelf, as well as the 1958 Geneva Convention on the Territorial Sea and Contiguous Zones which contains a similar provision on the delimitation of the territorial sea, based on the principle of equidistance. The government is also prepared to table the judgment of the International Court of Justice in the 1969 North Sea Continental Shelf cases.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, unless I am mistaken, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) will be tabling a green paper in the near future which will deal, I believe, with the principle of production of papers by the government. We can then study the matter with the opposition and finally come to a conclusion that will be satisfactory to all hon. members as well as the public which, from time to time, needs those papers

either to do some research, or to prepare basic papers in the fields which may exist within the federal government which, as we know, are extremely vast.
I should of course be very happy to answer the hon. member for South Shore otherwise, and to supply him with the papers he wants but, at this time, as I said at the beginning of my remarks, we are willing to supply all sorts of papers, the ones I mentioned and others if need be. Still, it is now impossible for us to table the papers dealing with the negotiations with the United States, France and Denmark. It is most unfortunate, Mr. Speaker, that we cannot meet the hon. member's request. Had it been possible, we should have been extremely pleased to do so.

speechtext: Just prior to the private members' hour the House had completed its consideration of the report stage of Bill C-9, so we shall now move on to another order of business. Bill C-48.

The House resumed consideration from Friday, April 22, of the motion of Mr. Marchand (for the Minister of Finance) that Bill C-48, to amend the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the Small Businesses Loans Act and the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE LOANS TO $75,000 FOR IMPROVEMENT OF FARMS, BUSINESSES OR FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a pleasure for me to take part in the debate concerning a piece of legislation to assist the small businessman, because such legislation is far too rarely before us for consideration. Even this bill, Bill C-48, to amend the Small Businesses Loans Act, the Farm Improvement Loans Act and the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act is actually an extension of legislation which first came into effect in 1961. Hon. members are aware that this legislation would expire automatically on June 30 of the current year in the absence of the amendments which are now before us. I therefore welcome
April 28, 1977

the bill and can only hope it will not take another three years before a piece of legislation dealing specifically with small business sees the light of day in this Chamber.
I mentioned the period of three years because it is at the end of three years that the act will next come up for review-the exact date is, in fact, June, 1980. Unfortunately the small business community cannot depend solely on the Small Businesses Loans Act and its triennial update. The small business community cannot, ,as it were, continue to hang in while governments in general ignore its basic needs on one hand and swamp it with bureaucratic regulations, directives, controls, forms, and general paperwork on the other. The small firms sector is what the free enterprise system in this country was built on, and if we want this system as we know it to continue to exist, much more must be done by way of the promotion and development of wide ranging programs and policies.
1 have said over and over again in this House as well as outside it that the government must commit itself to developing an over-all policy to assist the small business community in dealing with a broad range of issues and concerns. The party to which 1 belong has on many occasions put forward realistic recommendations for consideration by the government in dealing with this vital industrial sector. Indeed, just a month ago, on March 28, a private member's motion in my name was debated in this House at which time a whole series of ideas, recommendations, and specific suggestions were made by myself and by other members of the official opposition. We outlined in detail the necessity of allowing tax credits for investment in small business. We outlined in detail the necessity of providing assistance in the formation of small business export consortia.
It was ironic that I was able to take part yesterday in the debate dealing with the Export Development Act. I will quote one sentence I said in this regard:
It is unfortunate that there does not exist in the act or in this amendment a condition in the guarantee which would include a reasonable portion of the guarantee to be subcontracted to small and medium size industries in Canada.
This is a typical example of what the government policy is and has been in the past, but I hope will not continue to be in the future. Whenever the government deals with enterprise and with the economy, all legislation is always geared toward the same sector, that sector being the multinational large enterprises, many of them not even Canadian-owned. I have no concerns about that. My concern is that none of the legislation is geared toward the vast small and medium size community which is responsible for over 60 per cent of the labour force in Canada today. The Export Development Act, for example, is a perfect vehicle which could provide assistance in the formation of small and medium size enterprise export consortia. That is not happening. There is no indication from the government to include any of the export agencies to deal with small business. The EDC acts, helps, and assists roughly 20 to 25 large multinational corporations in Canada. That is why hundreds of millions of dollars are spent. It is very necessary, I admit; but
Improvement Loans
until we broaden the scope of this assistance we will be far behind the other industrialized nations of the world.
We have also made specific recommendations, and I believe this to be of vital importance, that the government change its tendering practices so that small business supplies a portion of government purchased goods and services. This is a long-established practice in the United States where it has been very effective. The small business community is competitive enough and there are enough sales both in respect to goods and services that governments can offer tendering opportunities to the small business community. Of course as far back as 1972 this party was advocating the necessity of substantially reducing the government's paperwork burden imposed on small business.
In this bill before us one of the amendments will increase from $50,000 to a maximum of $75,000 the principal amount of the loans under all three acts, namely, the Small Businesses Loans Act, Farm Improvement Loans Act, and the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. Naturally we welcome this amendment. Any amendment or any bill for the support of small business is welcome.
This is just one other example of the specific recommendation which we have been making for some time on this side of the House. As a matter of fact during that same debate on my motion on March 28, prior to the introduction of this bill, my colleague, the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington), put on record this specific recommendation. I will quote from page 4398 of Hansard which reads:
I also think that after having gone through an era of a very high rate of inflation the amount of the loan $50,000, should be increased to at least $75,000 and perhaps even to $100,000. Perhaps also that should come up for annual review.
In view of the inflation we have been through, and if the Minister of State (Small Business) (Mr. Marchand) is recommending changes to the Small Businesses Loans Act, perhaps he should give consideration to increasing the gross volume of business for firms qualifying under that act. I suggest that we look at something in the order of $1.5 million.
Strangely enough the next day the Minister of State (Small Business) (Mr. Marchand) announced that he would introduce amendments under the Small Businesses Loans Act using nearly the exact words of the hon. member for Capilano. I quote from the minister's own press release the day after, which reads:
More money will be available under the Small Businesses Loans Act and more businesses will qualify under planned changes to it, Small Business Minister Len Marchand said Monday. The biggest loan now available under the act is $50,000. But the government is considering increasing this to $75,000 or perhaps $100,000, Marchand said ...
When the minister spoke on this bill last Friday he indicated that the interest rates on these loans would be tied to a rate somewhere between 1 per cent and 2 per cent above prime. Those are the very words the hon. member for Capilano used a month earlier in that same speech. I will quote again from Hansard at page 4398 when he said:
I suggest that that rate above prime should be in the order of 1.25 per cent to 1.75 per cent so that we do not again get into the situation we have experienced whereby we have fixed the rate and removed the incentive from chartered banks to involve themselves in government guaranteed loans.

April 28, 1977
Improvement Loans
Strangely enough one of the minister's own colleagues, the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Cafik), in response to our recommendations in this regard of increasing interest rates had this to say, and I quote from Hansard at page 4401:
I, for one, take exception to a point raised by the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington). I enjoyed his remarks. He said that he would prefer it if the Small Businesses Loans Act would allow the banks to charge higher interest rates. That may make sense at first, but does not make sense when one examines the idea in depth. I think there is a better way to provide assistance than that suggested by the hon. member. The government assumes the risk of those loans; therefore I do not see why a bank should be entitled to as much interest as when it assumes the risk itself. It makes no sense.
He went on to say:
... the law should require the banks to devote a minimum percentage of loans to the small business community. And these loans should not be charged at rip-off interest rates, either, as implied in my honourable friend's suggestion.
This was one of the minister's own colleagues speaking at the very same time that this bill was being drawn up by the government. It is just another example of the so-called unanimity within the Liberal administration on the other side.
The point I am trying to make here, with all these quotes and comparisons, is a simple one, yet I believe a most important one at the same time. I call this a motherhood issue because nothing has been done for so long that anything within reason that is implemented by a government for the benefit of this sector is hailed as a breakthrough. The point is that it is too bad, in fact it is a shame, and kind of a waste to the people of Canada, that our political system has to be a game, instead of the government encouraging opposition members to participate positively through the simple incentive of thanks or even a slight word of recognition. These amendments that are before us now-and I have proved by the various quotes from members on this side prior to the introduction of the bill-are a typical example of recommendations being made by the official opposition and utilized by the government in such a devious way as to make it look as if it were done by it.
We do not mind if the government borrows or steals some of our recommendations. It is known for its flip-flops. Wage and price controls are one of its most famous flip-flops. But there are so many flip-flops that the government does not know whether it is flipping or flopping these days any longer.

speechtext: We never borrow any of your ideas.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE LOANS TO $75,000 FOR IMPROVEMENT OF FARMS, BUSINESSES OR FISHERIES
speechtext:
You borrowed this one. The honourable member said: "We never borrow any of your ideas". He could not have been listening when I quoted the specific recommendations of this party. But we do not mind. As a matter of fact, so far as small business is concerned, this vital sector of the economy can no longer wait for government action and the government should take into consideration some of our recommendations. 1 have heard none coming from the government side, yet we have made recommendations time and again, several of which I have listed in my remarks this evening.

Having said that, even though we agree these amendments are for the good of the business community and for Canada generally, they do not go far enough to achieve their objective. The government boasts that this bill is an improvement and will increase eligibility from $1 million to $1.5 million of gross sales, and increase from $50,000 to a maximum of $75,000 the principal amount of all loans made under the act. But this is merely keeping pace with inflation. Had these amendments not come before the House and the old levels remained, the small business community would have been robbed by the amount of increased inflation over the last three years. So basically what we are doing here is keeping up with inflation.
I believe this bill should have offered a lot more than it has, such as higher maximums, higher annual gross revenues for eligibility, an increase in the number of institutions offering these loans other than chartered banks, and a far greater variety of reasons qualifying people for loans, not only those engaged in small business but in the area of farm improvements and fisheries as well. I am not going to dwell on this matter because I look forward to bringing forward these recommendations perhaps by way of amendments when the bill reaches committee stage.
If the government is serious about trying to assist the small business community, then it will have to dedicate itself to the betterment of that community along the lines adopted by the United States Congress. The United States Congress has a declared policy to support small and medium enterprises. It has a small business administration with a mandate to achieve certain goals and objectives, all of which are contributing to a far better economic climate, one we can never hope to have in this country unless we set our goals and our sights in a similar direction. The government cannot deal with a complex situation like the small and medium size enterprise sector on an ad hoc basis. An over-all policy must be established, perhaps in the form of a small business act, something which is drastically missing.
Nearly one year ago, I believe, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) appointed a minister of state responsible for small business. I suggest we are 20 years behind other industrialized nations. Every other industrialized nation in the world appoints a minister responsible for small business. In view of the record of this government in regard to its creation of "sub-ministers", I do not have very much faith in the appointment of the Minister of State (Small Business). It can be compared with the Prime Minister's appointment of a minister of multiculturalism prior to the 1974 election. Since the ethnic people of Canada were discontented with some of the attitudes of the government, in order to appease this large group of new Canadians the Prime Minister appointed a minister responsible for multiculturalism. We all know what happened to that minister and to that department; they disappeared as soon as the government received a mandate in the 1974 election. I hope the intention is not the same regarding the minister in charge of small business.
April 28, 1977

As I have said, government policy in the shape of an act must be established in the near future if we are to change the situation and find solutions which potentially exist. The first step in the establishment of such a policy or act must be to define the portfolio of the minister of state in charge of small business, a definition which can universally be used as a working definition by other government departments which deal from time to time with the problems of small businessmen. When I asked several months ago whether the Minister of State (Small Business) had such a definition, he had to admit he had not. I doubt very much whether the government has any intention of establishing a definition which would form the basis of potential policy or a small business act, hence my reservations about the intentions of the government.
I realize the difficulty that the minister himself is having in attempting to pull the many loose ends together. His is not an easy job since a small business portfolio has never existed before in this country. He is also attempting at the same time to act as a sort of liaison between the many departments having to do with small business from time to time. I am sure he is working in good faith within his own portfolio, and although I know he has travelled diligently across the country on behalf of small business, as I have, if I have to fault him personally in any way it would have to be for not yet having travelled abroad to other industrialized nations to compare the situations there and learn how far behind we are in the area of small business.
I have had the opportunity to visit West Germany to attend a small business symposium. I have been to Washington to meet with members of the small business administration. I have had the opportunity of travelling to Japan where I met with the director general of the small and medium enterprise agency. I have compared programs which we could follow. There is nothing wrong with borrowing successful programs and implementing them in this country. Since I have had an opportunity of studying these programs I am in the position of being able to make recommendations to the minister.
I wish the minister had had the same opportunity as I to travel to these industrialized capitals of the world, instead of only having one trip abroad as minister responsible for small business. He visited Moscow in the Soviet Union; perhaps he was studying their new capitalist system or free enterprise system! As 1 say, we must examine successful programs in other nations and borrow their policies. Japan has a small and medium enterprise agency, the United States has a small business administration. West Germany, Belgium and others have similar agencies and administrations dedicated to the betterment of their industrial way of life. We have no such administration.
I hope that interested groups such as chambers of commerce across the country, the Canadian Manufacturers Association, and the Canadian Federation of Independent Businesses will put sufficient pressure on the government so it takes the initiatives and develops small business policy emcompassing all of the areas affected by the small business community. The small businessman on his own is not powerful enough to lobby
Improvement Loans
the government in the way the large multinational corporations are. The small businessman whether in the east, the west, northern Ontario, Quebec City or anywhere else in Canada, has the same problems. It is one of the biggest areas of unity in this country. The same problems are faced by all these people, but they cannot deal with them alone. I urge the interested groups to continue to bring pressure on the government to improve its thinking with regard to this important industrial aspect.
As I said before, my concern is so genuine regarding the problems of small business and freedom of enterprise that I hope the seriousness of these problems and the potential solutions, some of which I have mentioned, can be dealt with on a non-partisan basis. It is only possible on a number of issues in this country, small business being one of them. We cannot wait any longer to move in a positive direction in this regard. I hope all members realize the seriousness of this situation, as I know the Minister of State for Small Business has realized it, but unfortunately he does not have sufficient powers as yet-and I use the word "yet" advisedly because I hope this will come-to convince the cabinet that small business in the field of economics is a major area of importance which has been overlooked by the government for far too long. At least more of us now have began to talk about the issue- that is an improvement.
When in the late 1960's as a small businessman I first started making public pronouncements, recommendations, and suggestions voicing the concerns of the small business community, we were not talking about the issue at that time. There is an improvement now; we are at least beginning to talk about it. In many cases we have begun to listen as well. The government must have been listening in order to come up with this piece of legislation because it did not come up with these recommendations before taking them from us. It is not until the government commits itself to action in this regard that we will stop losing the diminishing opportunities for small business that still exist in the field of economics and free enterprise.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE LOANS TO $75,000 FOR IMPROVEMENT OF FARMS, BUSINESSES OR FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, following along the same lines as my colleague, I want to begin my remarks by saying that certainly we will support this bill, but that is not to say that we are wholeheartedly in agreement with it. When I saw the bill for the first time I was flabbergasted, and I asked my colleagues to look at it. It is so flimsy that it could not possibly contain all the things that we should be doing to support and bolster the small business community in Canada. However, I have to support the bill because this is a part of what we in the official opposition have been asking for over the past few years.
I accept the proposal to raise the limits on loans and on what would constitute a small business. In light of today's inflation and of the cost of doing business it is proper that we should raise our sights and recognize the fact that any business with an annual volume of $1.5 million is actually a small business.

April 28, 1977
Improvement Loans
It would not have been out of line to raise that limit to $2 million when one takes into consideration the loss in inflation. I am not sure that raising the limit on borrowing from $50,000 to $75,000 is going far enough to catch up with the changing economic picture in Canada and elsewhere. Raising it to $100,000 might have been more realistic and would have been less than 10 per cent of the volume of business allowable to qualify as a small business under the terms of the act.
Again let me commend the Minister of State (Small Business) (Mr. Marchand) for bringing in this bill. I understand it is for a three year term, and if the amounts do not seem large enough I hope he will go to cabinet and ask them to reconsider the figures even during the term of the bill before us.
Speaking in terms of the tourist business, a business that is of more than just passing interest in my area of Parry Sound-Muskoka, you cannot do very much with $75,000 today. It would not buy you very much in the way of tourist facilities and it would not go very far in upgrading tourist facilities. In my area there are many resorts that would be better attractions if they could afford to refurbish and upgrade their facilities. There are many businesses in my area which would like to expand or modernize their establishments, but they are faced with the prospect of a continued decline in tourism.
As most hon. members are aware, Canada's tourist balance has been tilted in favour of the United States over the past few years and even in favour of countries overseas. Last year we had a deficit in our tourist balance of almost $1.5 million. This is a lot of lost dollars and a lot of unhappy businessmen and tourist operators.
When I think of small businesses and this proposed legislation to aid the small business community I have to think of the small businesses in my riding which depend on tourism to survive, and of the thousands of people in the riding who depend on those small businesses for their seasonal employment. When those people cannot depend on tourist jobs in the summer it makes for a pretty lean year for them, and far too many of my people had just such a lean year in the past year. I want something better for them and I know that we are capable of providing something better. I am also aware that a great many of the other ridings are in the same predicament.
When I saw this bill I knew it would not contain many recommendations that we in the official opposition have been pressing for over the past three or four years. However, I suggest it is simply a means of looking after the immediate problems in the hope that we would accept these provisions and not come back demanding more. If that is so, then it is a vain hope. I do not intend to let up on my fight to have something in the way of a small business administration in Canada along the lines of the small business administration in the United States. We need it, and I will continue to demand it.
My colleague, the hon. member for High Park-Humber Valley (Mr. Jelinek), mentioned the assistance provided by the U.S. government for small businessmen. Certainly they could use it in my area. We have a golden opportunity to draw on the small business act in the United States. We do not even
have to break new ground. We only have to study the record and success of this act and take from it the things that would apply directly to our own situation and our own needs, and adapt them to our own system. There is no doubt that the small business administration in the U.S. has been an unqualified success.
There are people who scoff at the idea of borrowing anything from our neighbour to the south, and possibly the socialists and the supranationalists would be included among them. They will tell you that we will lose our identity if we borrow any techniques and expertise from the United States and that we should guard our purity from the Yankees. To those people I simply say, "Nonsense, pull your head out of the sand." It is time for action to get our small business community in high gear and get our economy on the move again.
I might sound repetitious but I will take that risk and repeat that small businesses in Canada provide more than 55 per cent of the jobs in our country. They account for more than 50 per cent of the dollar value of business conducted in our country, and that is no small amount. Taken as an economic unit the small business community is the single most important economic community in our country. That is surely reason enough to look upon this unit with more than just passing interest. We have to look upon it as the most important tool in the fight against unemployment. We have to look upon it as the most important lever to get our economy moving again.
The two items in this bill affecting small business are just not enough. There is still no indication that the government is going to give the Minister of State (Small Business) the tools and the latitude he needs to become the effective minister he could be and should be.
It must be pretty frustrating for that very capable minister to know that he is severely limited in his ability to provide leadership to the small business people of our country. I sincerely hope that the appointment of the minister to such an important post does not turn out to be merely window dressing.
I presume the minister is engaged in other important matters this evening, or he would be here. I am quite sure he is interested in quick passage of this bill.
Bill C-48 will carry on the Small Businesses Loans Act for three years following June 30. As I mentioned before, it certainly has some good points. To date I believe $480 million has been lent out as small business loans since the inception of the act back in about 1961. While close to half a billion dollars is a lot money, spread over that number of years I do not think it is very much. If that figure were compared with the number of applications, I am sure there would have been many applicants who were not able to avail themselves of the benefits which will again be made available under this very worthwhile bill.
I have some figures which are worth-while putting on the record once again. There is a total of 329,000 small businesses throughout Canada. Of these, 137,000 are classified wholesale; 32,000 construction; 46,000 manufacturing; 37,000 service

April 28, 1977

industries; 56,000 transportation and warehousing; 13,000 are apartment owners; and 8,000 are owners of other buildings but still classified small businesses. Many of these businesses have applied for small business loans through chartered banks and have been told that funds were not available and that the allocated amount for such and such a chartered bank or such and such a branch had been used up. However, they were told that money would be available at regular interest rates, which are 2 per cent and sometimes 3 per cent higher. I know many hon. members have been faced with this problem.
Businessmen have written asking about the preferred small business loan and how to go about getting it, and hon. members write back telling them to go to their own bank branches and how to approach their bank managers. This is frustrating for them, and they come back to their members of parliament wanting to know what to do because it is just a joke. I have received dozens of letters from very disgruntled businessmen who have approached their banks and asked for loans.
At one time the loans were at a much lower interest rate. I believe the current rate is 9.5 per cent. We know that in the past year or two the rate was not realistic because banks could hardly be expected to lend money at the prime rate. So although the interest rate is not stipulated in this bill-it will probably be proclaimed by order in council or in some other way-I hope it will be attractive.
I have received some caustic comments from some people in this regard. They complain that they go to the bank and borrow money at 12 per cent. We tell them that they can get money under the Small Businesses Loans Act for 9.5 per cent, but there is no money. We read in the paper that the Government of Canada is lending money to Third World countries, and one example has been thrown at me on different occasions. Perhaps other hon. members have received the same complaint, that is, that the government was lending money to Cuba at 3 per cent and that it should lend money to its own citizens at a more attractive interest rate than the going rate.
I know a great many businessmen who are hard up and who are trying to get money for working capital. I know they have not been able to avail themselves of it through this particular channel, but the important thing for them is to get the money, period. A good many are willing to pay almost any rate, so they borrow money from finance companies, and most of us know that finance companies borrow their money at a very high rate of interest and lend it out at an even higher rate. We find some small businessmen paying 14 per cent, 15 per cent and even more in order to keep going and to get working capital. That is a real hardship for them.
Small businessmen are frustrated by the red tape demanded by the federal government, and possibly provincial governments as well. There are forms which have to be filled out. Sales have to be divulged, and so do various other business activities. Time and again small businesses have had to hire people who should actually be on the payroll of the government because all they do is provide information to various levels of government. Perhaps the government could give some consideration to sending these forms out on, shall we say, a hit
Improvement Loans
and miss basis instead of to every small business. In this way, like the Gallup Poll, the government could get the information it needs without demanding it from every small businessman from Newfoundland to British Columbia. Small businessmen are required to fill out these forms on pain of fines and, I suppose, imprisonment, and that is certainly frustrating to them.
I see that the Postmaster General (Mr. Blais) is here. I received a letter from a businessman in Huntsville which says: "I am interested in opening a small mail order business and wish to direct questions to the Minister of Small Business." I have written the minister and given him the necessary information. The writer of this letter is a real optimist because his business is going to depend on the Post Office.

I have a great deal of respect for the Postmaster General who represents the riding adjacent to mine; that is, of course, with certain reservations. During the last Post Office strike prior to Christmas of 1975 a great many small businessmen were put out of business. That happened during one strike, and it was really crippling. Big business could roll with the punch and hire their own carriers. Which was the biggest hiring carrier during the strike? The government, you bet your life. It could get on without the Post Office, but the little John Smith and all the other small citizens of the country, they could not get along without the Post Office. Mr. Speaker, the Post Office provides an important service, which we hope will improve.
The Postmaster General may be interested to know that last week I had the privilege of being in London, England, to investigate the operations of the British postal service. Although the British postal service, according to the British themselves, is not the best in the world, it is not the worst either. When I told English people in this country that 1 was going to England to examine the postal service, they laughed in my face. Similarly, when my colleague, the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale), was in the United States to assess the postal service of that country for the purpose of being able to suggest to our Postmaster General how to improve this country's postal service, he was laughed at also. True, England is not as large as Canada. Nevertheless 93 per cent of first class mail is delivered the next day. That is a pretty good record.
