speechtext:
Perhaps the hon. member is right. I went to England to examine their postal service and to talk to their unions. After all, workers are most important in a post office operation and you cannot do the job unless the workers are behind you. Altogether there are 472,000 employees in the postal service of Great Britain, if you include telephone and telecommunications employees as well. I think the Post Office employs directly 117,000 workers. Mr. Speaker, over there workers sit down with management. They may sympathize with each other's views and try to iron out difficulties. 1 wish we could do that here. I know the Postmaster General is trying to improve the situation, and his efforts are important for the small businessman. I see you looking at me with a jaundiced eye, Mr. Speaker, as if I am out of order. Let me say that the postal service is important to all business but is the lifeblood of small business in this country.
A businessman may have the best product to sell, the best service to provide, the best reputation. Everything about his business may be about A-l. But if he cannot please his customers and he relies on the postal service, he will be out of luck if anything goes wrong with the service. Clearly, our Post Office provides an essential service.
I hope the Post Office will listen sympathetically to some of our union people, and when I say that I am not carrying the torch for that Scotsman, Joe Davidson; oh, no! The ordinary Post Office worker wants to do his job. In Great Britain the postmen take great pride in carrying the Queen's mail.
We also learned that the post office in Great Britain is a public corporation, not a government department as it is in Canada. I was surprised to learn that, thinking that at least the British post office would be a Crown corporation. But no, they call it a public corporation over there. I wanted to put that point on the record.
I say to the Postmaster General through you, Mr. Speaker, that the small businessman depends heavily on this country's postal service. In many cases the postal service can make or break a business. This bill will certainly help the small businessman obtain money, provided the businessman can qualify for loans. Certainly many will not qualify for loans; many businessmen cannot put up the proper security. That, of course, is the name of the game. They must at least show that they have enough security to show the banks, and the government, that they can pay the money back.
I commend the government for introducing this bill and hope it will be given quick passage. Certainly it will help farmers, and there are many farmers in Parry Sound-Muskoka who will want to avail themselves of money available under this legislation. One must not forget that the bill will also be of benefit to many commercial fishermen and make money available to them.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I hoped the Minister of State (Small Business) (Mr. Marchand) would be present this evening so that we could congratulate him and wish him well in his portfolio. The hon. member for High Park-Humber Valley (Mr. Jelinek) paid him a compliment. The minister has travelled across the country, getting in touch with small businessmen and learning their problems. He hopes to arrive at solutions. I note that the hon. member for High Park-Humber Valley was critical of the minister for visiting Russia. He went to that country to learn some of their business techniques. Certainly his visit extended his horizons, but whether he obtained any helpful information is another question.

speechtext: What? Do you expect to find small business in Russia?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE LOANS TO $75,000 FOR IMPROVEMENT OF FARMS, BUSINESSES OR FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I look on this bill as a piece of tokenism. It sets out a great deal of framework to help small businessmen but the substance is lacking. Is it not odd that we need to provide public assistance to fishermen, farmers, and small businessmen, the so-called backbone of private enterprise in Canada? Apparently our small enterprisers cannot get assistance from the big enterprisers, the large corporations, and must fall back on the government for assistance.
Actually I am proud that the government has taken the initiative of bringing forward this legislation which will help farmers. It will help them to finance their operations. It will help fishermen who face difficult times these days not only with respect to catches but with respect to financing, and it will help the small businessman. Small businessmen are becoming an ever-diminishing breed in Canada. If that
April 28, 1977

favoured phrase "private enterprise" is to have any meaning, we must take some initiative to help them.
Bill C-48 does three things. The loan limits in the three acts of parliament the bill seeks to amend are to be raised from $50,000 to $75,000 and the increased ceiling will be a help to fishermen, farmers, and small businessmen.
Second, it raises the eligibility requirement in defining small business enterprise from $1 million to $l'/2 million, which takes into account the pressures of inflation.
Third, it extends the period for which loans can be made under the three programs from July 1, 1977, to June 30, 1980. It also increases the aggregate amount of loans made in this period in which the minister would be liable for losses.
With regard to the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the minister would be liable for an increase from $1,400 million to $1,550 million; with regard to the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act from $70 million to $80 million; and with regard to the Small Business Loans Act from $350 million to $600 million.
We have watched a dramatic trend in Canada from small business to big business. In the past England used to be known as a nation of shopkeepers. We in Canada had a good mixture of farmers, fishermen, and businessmen. Now we see the development from small business to big business, and from big business to large corporations, mostly multinational corporations.
According to the 1971 figures, which are the latest figures available, we have 153,000 non-financial corporations in Canada, but 626, or 4 per cent, account for 63 per cent of the total business assets, 58 per cent of the total profits, and paid only 46 per cent of the taxes. That underlines the trend that has taken place in Canada and other countries throughout the world.
In Canada we have four companies which supply 80 per cent of the refined petroleum, four companies which supply 80 per cent of our flour, four companies which supply 95 per cent of our cars, and four companies which supply 80 per cent of our iron and steel. This trend destroys the concept of private enterprise. It eliminates competition, drives prices up, and places the key sector of the economy in the hands of monopolies and oligopolies.
There are three types of enterprise in Canada; private enterprise, public enterprise and co-operative enterprise. All members will agree that the last one, co-operative enterprise, has done an excellent job with regard to protecting certain groups in society. Western farmers had to band together in co-ops to protect themselves from high feed, grain and fertilizer prices. Only by doing this through the co-operative enterprise were they able to obtain prices that were reasonable.
Co-ops have played a very important part in the economy of Canada. I am sure that members from the maritimes can give dramatic instances of how co-ops have played a very important part in helping small business people.

In Saskatchewan they have a business assistance branch to help small business and it is part of the department of industry and commerce. The aim of this program in Saskatchewan is to improve the management of small business. It began in 1973 and its budget is gradually increasing as the branch demonstrates its worth. I have heard many members tell us that businessmen find difficulty in understanding the intent of legislation or with regard to filling out business forms. This department provides small businessmen with the necessary information and assistance.
The second area of activity is a business review program, commonly called counselling. Problems are identified and solutions found. Most of the clients referred for counselling have been in trouble and have been recommended by a bank or a municipality. It is important, if a man has gone to a bank and finds himself in trouble, that he can turn to a department of government for assistance. The work of this branch is co-ordinated with the Saskatchewan Economic Development Company-SECO. Mr. Speaker, if one takes a look at cocoons and the foliage of our country, or under the clapboards of old houses, one realizes there has been development and that eventually will emerge one of the beauties of life-to examine and explore the world as it is. I sometimes wonder when those on my left who live in cocoons, such as the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert), will ever come out of the cocoon and open their eyes to the world as it is.
I think we have to recognize in fairness to all political faiths in this country that the private enterprise system has developed a structure in which we can have a two car family, a structure which does not exist under those political regimes which those on my left would eulogize, praise, and try to copy, and then suggest to us that we should do the same. A human factor of this world which must be recognized is that there has to be incentive for the individual to produce. That incentive is best provided by the free enterprise system. The remarks of the hon. member were misleading and deceptive.
I do not say this by way of protecting our banking structure; I say it perhaps in condemnation of governmental policy over the years, but it is a fact that the rate of interest charged by any lending institution, whether it be a bank or any other institution, is established by, and related to, the rate set by the Bank of Canada. In the United States the rate is set by the Federal Reserve Board, and so on down the line. Lending institutions, whether publicly owned or privately owned, will certainly lend on the guidelines established by the federally controlled monetary system of this country. There is nothing that the Caisses Populaire, the co-operative, or any other financial structure in this land can do but lend at a rate related to the rate established by the Bank of Canada. Any statement to the contrary is intended to deceive and to destroy the confidence of our people and of our investors in our system.
This is not what this bill or any other bill in the House is all about, Mr. Speaker. This is a time when encouragement should be given to every sector of the economy to try to develop, to create employment, whether public or private. Suggestions that there is presently corporate welfare can only come from the mouths of those who have created policies which have created tax structures, which have created the impossible situation that exists for many corporate structures of this land.
The idea that small business is gobbled up by large business is one of the plights of business in New Brunswick. But this

started during the early stages of Confederation. It is still going on, and nothing that government has done can stop it. But much that government has done has accentuated it, and let us recognize what those things were.
First, there was the inheritance tax, which made it utterly and totally impossible for a family to retain in its possession the firm on which it had made its base and on which communities lived. The tax structure has compelled individuals to sell to larger, to smaller, or to other interests. But ownership has been transferred.
When the inheritance tax in many jurisdictions in this country disappeared, there was then a capital gains tax. There is one particular company in my province at the moment which, if it sells at all, will probably sell to a larger firm, and it may be wound up as an employer in our province. I deplore any tax structure which wipes out industry in an area of unemployment in excess of 10 per cent, 12 per cent or 15 per cent, as is the case in the Atlantic area.
Let us point the finger where it belongs, Mr. Speaker. Those families would hold those companies in perpetuity if the tax structure would permit. But it will not so permit, nor will it ever permit so long as government spends according to the course that this government has plotted. We need not speeches which will destroy confidence in this country; we need speeches which will encourage investment to relieve the unemployment structure. When one pleads for an unstable economy, as the hon. member for Broadview did, one is pleading the very opposite of the objective of his party, namely, curing unemployment. Let us get out of the cocoon and look at the real world. Let us try to re-establish confidence, not break it down.

Again this bill is a step in the right direction, but I should like to point out that many equipment costs and building costs within the farming structure have doubled in this four year period. Labour costs have more than doubled, fuel costs have more than doubled, and in one year alone the cost of pesticides went up 50 per cent. I asked for a farm improvement loan and 1 was told bluntly and directly that in that particular branch no farm improvement loans would be made to me or to any other farmer because it was the manager's responsibility to create maximum profit in that branch and he could not do it by means of farm improvement, home improvement or comparable types of loans. This decision should not rest in the hands of a small village bank manager. His decision can make or break the small businessman, the farmer or the fisherman. 1 implore the government to give consideration to that suggestion.
We have been accused on many occasions by members of all parties in the House of not making concrete suggestions. I submit this one to you for consideration. Let us see what the government will do with it when it is passed directly to it.
When we get down to the fisheries aspect of this legislation, we find that the increase of $70 million to $80 million does not cover one year's increment in government requirements. If the

rate of increment in this ceiling had compared with the rate of increase in government spending in all but one of the past four years, this could have been increased for just one year by more than $10 million. The Postmaster General (Mr. Blais) injected a few remarks so perhaps, Mr. Speaker, you would permit me to answer them. I want to place on the record tonight that 20 years ago if a letter were mailed in the morning from Ottawa it would be in my community the next day at noon. Today, if I mail a letter to my community, it might arrive in two days, five days or ten days, and it will be five or more days more often than it will be one day. So if the Postmaster General has the unadulterated audacity to interject, regardless of earlier comments in any postal discussion, let him say what he plans to do to return the postal service to at least the standard of the days of the horse and wagon or the stagecoach, because we are presently below that level of postal service in Canada today, particularly in the constituency of Carleton-Charlotte. It is a disgrace at best.
Apparently mail is piled in a corner and left for further consideration when somebody has time to take it out and put it on the rails, on an airplane, or somewhere. This has been detrimental to business, small and large, and particularly to small business. Let me give you one example. It has been impossible for people in my constituency to receive statements from Toronto and get them back by return mail without having passed the due date, so interest charges are imposed if the terms are less than ten days. That is the impact of the type of mail service we have. It should go from Toronto to the Saint John valley in one day and back the next, but it cannot be done, and both big and small businesses are paying a high price to try to accommodate the needs of society.
Let us do everything that can be done not to dampen the spirit of investment, not to dampen the spirit of free enterprise, and not to discourage the development of productive public enterprise if that be the wish of some in the House; but let us get this bill on the rails with reasonable limits and with at least compulsion on lenders to submit the applications to some authority. subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-ALLEGATION WAGE SETTLEMENTS MADE ABOVE GUIDELINES-GOVERNMENT POSITION

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-ALLEGATION WAGE SETTLEMENTS MADE ABOVE GUIDELINES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise this evening as a result of a question I asked and an answer given by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) on April 20, 1977, with respect to the position of the Treasury Board regarding its settlements in excess of the 8 per cent guidelines of the controls program in the public sector.
At the time the minister was unaware of the specific settlements to which I referred which exceeded the 8 per cent guidelines set down for all Canadians. For the minister's information I refer-and I have given notice to his office and to him-to some of the examples 1 raised at that time, namely, the welfare programs group which was given a raise of 8.66 per cent, financial administration employees whose raise ave-
Adjournment Debate
raged 9.08 per cent, the office equipment group which received an increase of 8.7 per cent, and the general technical workers who were allowed an 8.92 per cent salary increase. Generally speaking, these increases were given during the course of this year for the future year, that is to say, not in the first year but in a subsequent, second or third year of the anti-inflation program.
While there is no doubt that the four wage settlements are in excess of the 6 per cent plus 2 per cent wage increase guideline for the second year of the anti-inflation program, the Treasury Board has applied an exempting clause in the AIB regulations to allow a settlement higher than the basic rate. Section 48 of the regulations allows an experience adjustment factor of plus or minus 2 per cent to compensate for groups whose wages have either fallen behind or surged ahead of an agreed benchmark during the period preceding controls. The benchmark is obtained by adding 2 per cent to the rate of increase in the Consumer Price Index over either the previous two years or the period of the last collective agreement, whichever is greater. In simpler terms, if a group's wage increases were below inflation plus productivity, they are compensated. By this measure, the four groups were deemed to have fallen behind and were granted increases in excess of the basic guideline. Because this procedure is specified in the AIB regulations, the settlements appear to be within the AIB arithmetic guideline.
I expect the parliamentary secretary who this evening is to speak on behalf of the minister to say roughly what I just said. Perhaps I anticipated his answer; I wanted to make his job easier for him this evening. I note he is wearing a somewhat strange-looking T-shirt. 1 am fully aware of the facts, but 1 am anxious to hear his comments on this important matter. If the parliamentary secretary's answer is along the lines of the comments I made just now, I think it can be said that it would evade some issues which are central to the example the federal government ought to set for Canadians.
First, it should be noted that in none of the four cases on which the question was based does the experience adjustment factor approach the yearly maximum of 2 per cent. Since the minimum previous period to which the adjustment applies is two years, one can conclude that in none of these cases was the loss in excess of 1 per cent per year. In fact the highest experience adjustment entitlement was for the financial administration group at 1.5 per cent, who settled for a 9.05 per cent wage increase. In other words, at worst this group fell behind 0.75 per cent a year from the national benchmark. At no time did any of the four groups actually experience a reduction in purchasing power due to prices rising faster than wages.
The settlements in excess of the strict six plus two guideline are to compensate for these groups not obtaining in the past their share of the gains in national productivity. Whether the public service contributes to gains in productivity is questionable indeed. But beyond that, whether groups within the public

April 28, 1977
Adjournment Debate
service should be allowed to exceed the strict guideline when they have not lost purchasing power to inflation is even more questionable, particularly when the federal government ought to be setting the example.
The eight plus two experience calculation is, of course, the wage settlement ceiling under the AIB regulations. But these four cases indicate that the formula is also the wage settlement floor. There is no obligation, explicit or implicit, in the AIB regulations for employers to pay up to the maximum allowable. The reason that Treasury Board is willing to permit wage increases at or near the arithmetic guidelines appears to be that the policy of wage comparability still holds sway in the Treasury Board. Arguing that federal wage settlements have been below those in the private sector, the minister has stated a commitment to maintain "all elements of compensation in the public service ... in an equitable relationship with compensation levels in the private sector."
Maintaining the wage comparability policy throughout the controls program amounts to a signal to wage negotiators in the private sector that the dispute over income shares can continue. It was to halt such disputes that wage controls were introduced. And, indeed, the Anti-Inflation Board has indicated that it will be less tolerant in the second and third years of the program of wage requests appealing to such notions as historical relationship and comparability.
I think the parliamentary secretary is obliged to tell the House the government's position with respect to public sector settlements. Does he, speaking on behalf of the government, not feel that there is a responsibility resting on the government to show leadership in wage increase restraint? In view of increases which have been granted, is the strict six plus two upper guideline still to be enforced, or will the government take the position in future public service wage settlements that past settlements failed to compensate fully for increases in the cost of living? I wish the parliamentary secretary would answer my questions in this regard.
Mr. Bob Kaplan (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of
Finance): Mr. Speaker, I was rather surprised to note that the hon. member, in asking his question, spent four or five of his seven minutes answering his own question.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-ALLEGATION WAGE SETTLEMENTS MADE ABOVE GUIDELINES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: I know the answer. I wanted to hear the parliamentary secretary give his version of his answer.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-ALLEGATION WAGE SETTLEMENTS MADE ABOVE GUIDELINES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Certainly 1 assure the hon. member that the government is well aware that on the part of the public there is considerable concern that wage settlements within the public service should not be a signal to the private sector to increase settlements. They should not increase settlements or set a lead in the rate of wage settlements. However, wage settlements within the public service should be comparable. Certainly public servants should not be made the scapegoat in the battle against inflation. We have no intention of doing that. However, we feel that there are a number of elements in the private sector which have regarded public service settlements as taking a lead. That is not the intention or the policy of the govern-
[Mr. Hnatyshyn.)
ment. On the contrary, we feel that public servants are entitled to comparable wages for comparable work, but settlements within the public sector ought not to set the pace for settlement within the private sector.
To comply with the anti-inflation program, the permissible increase in total compensation for a group for any guideline year is the sum of the following items: first, the basic protection factor, which is a percentage increase, represents the maximum that a group may obtain during the AIB program. This total compensation percentage increase varies from year to year. In the first program year, it is set at 8 per cent; in the second year it is set at 6 per cent maximum; in the third year it is set at 4 per cent maximum.
Second, the national productivity factor, which is added to the basic protection factor, is equated to an estimated annual increase in the Canadian productivity which is set at 2 per cent for each year of the program.
Third, the experience adjustment factor results from the previous collective agreement for a group. Movements in the total compensation for that group should compare to the movements in the consumer price index for the same period of time, that is, the length of the previous agreement. The maximum value of the experience adjustment factor is set at 2 per cent for each year of the program and, in its calculation, may result in a plus or minus 2 per cent depending on the extent to which the consumer price index has increased compared to total compensation.

subtopic: HEALTH-POSSIBILITY OF BANNING PRODUCTS IN ADDITION TO SACCHARIN THAT MAY BE DANGEROUS TO HEALTH
HEALTH-POSSIBILITY OF BANNING PRODUCTS IN ADDITION TO SACCHARIN THAT MAY BE DANGEROUS TO HEALTH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 22 I questioned the arbitrary decision of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) to ban saccharin, a ban without reference to any studies on humans or without approval of this House. It had all the earmarks of a bureaucratic decision. It was based on a pretext, I maintain a phony pretext, of science. It was forced on this nation.
There are many obvious reasons to distrust the ban. The pretense of scientific rationale has made Canadians the joke of the international medical community. The non-medical community would also be amused if they were not, like myself, so angered.
The ban reflects the whole ridiculousness and arrogance of a certain few senior bureaucrats. It is a decision that will endanger the lives of 400,000 Canadian diabetics, tens of thousands of victims of hypoglycemia and possibly ten million or 12 million citizens with propensity to overweight or obesity with all their health hazards.
My question was, and I quote:
In view of the fact that excessive amounts of saccharin have been found dangerous to rats and it is to be banned for human consumption, and it should be
April 28, 1977

noted that humans have built-in protection in that they would drown before contacting cancer using comparable amounts, will the minister advise the House whether we can expect his medical researchers to push ahead to ban chocolate, ice cream, cheese, liver, milk, eggs, coconut, sugar, salt and all other products that induce high cholesterol and heart disease to humans, even though we are not sure if it is safe for rats? ... Further, will he also consider banning cars, also dangerous to humans, although we have no statistics on rat mortality?
It is interesting to note that the minister at that time referred to the statements of his officials. That is where it is at. The officials make the decisions in this country. The public fears the officials, not the members of parliament. They have to follow the whims of these people.
The hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) asked why cigarettes had not been banned since there is conclusive evidence they induced cancer in people. Constituents have asked me the same question. Petitions have poured in, by way of the distinguished radio personality, Roy Jacks, urging that the ban not be invoked.
In reply to my letters on behalf of constituents and these petitioners I received the most ridiculous reply, dated April 22, obviously written in justification for his decision by the official who apparently provides the answers for the minister when the estimates are before the committee. If I can find it, I will read part of it into the record:
As to cigarette smoking, unfortunately, however, a ban on tobacco simply would not have the desired effect. Cigarette smoking represents a form of addiction which has become over the years not only tolerated by large segments of our sociey but also has become incorporated into the lifestyle of many of our citizens.
That is an answer which is a total evasion. Yet they ban something which is essential to the nation and the protection of thousands of people.
Then again, the word "scientific" is used very loosely. It is remarkable they should use the word "may" and still call it a scientific reply. It is hardly scientific not to use absolutes. The excuse for the ban is the protection of the public. We once feared the invasion of the privacy of the nation's bedrooms but it now seems quite acceptable for the Department of National Health and Welfare not only to invade the privacy of the nation's dinner table, but to endanger the lives of many who need and want sweetened foods. They say, "Take heart, dear one. Oh, we care. Just pick up your saccharin tablets or powder from the pharmacist after October." But those who need or want saccharin ask, as I ask, where they will get the sweetness and joy from a dull, restrictive diet when they can no longer purchase diet pop, candy, cookies, canned foods, chocolate, gum and all the rest?
The experiments on which the ban was based are treated, and quite properly treated, with contempt by most of the public and by many thinking medical people, including the British and Swiss medical associations. What is so disgraceful about this whole situation is that those who literally survive because of saccharin, and have done so for many years, have been frightened by superficial reports with regard to findings which are not even worthy of discussion.
Adjournment Debate
Rats were given massive doses of saccharin. The experiments in Canada and in the United States began with 5 per cent of the rats' daily diet by weight. When there was not much evidence on which to support what would seem to be a determined effort to prove that artificial sweeteners were dangerous, dosages were increased by 50 per cent to 7.5 per cent on 100 rats. In the first generation three out of 100 rats developed some sign or form of carcinoma. It is remarkable, I realize now, that of their offspring only ten out of 100 developed it. If they gave the same dosage to the baby rats it meant that naturally those rats would get very sick.
To get an equivalent amount, a human being would have to consume 800 cans of soda pop for the rest of his or her life each day, or ingest about 10,000 grains of saccharin a day. Honourable members will see the bottle I am holding up. It contains 1,000 half-grain capsules. They would have to take 20 of these a day and that would be the equivalent of 40,000 teaspoons a day in sweeteners. How ridiculous that experiment was! There is no way in which a human being can consume the equivalent of what the rats had to take. I think the sugar combines have been a part of this whole thing-

subtopic: INCOME TAX-EXEMPTIONS FOR MAINTENANCE ORDERS- DISCRIMINATION AGAINST THOSE MADE FOR COMMON LAW SPOUSES
INCOME TAX-EXEMPTIONS FOR MAINTENANCE ORDERS- DISCRIMINATION AGAINST THOSE MADE FOR COMMON LAW SPOUSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I rise at such a time, on such an occasion, and in such vast company, I realize that being a member of an opposition party can sometimes not only be a lonely job but can also be a singular job.
The task that brings me here this evening relates to something that I thought had been covered some time back, but which was not. This is about a young black person who worked in construction and who came to me with his income tax request. It appeared that a number of years back he had entered into a common law relationship, as a result of which he had two children. He had broken up that relationship and is now in a regular marriage, and he has other obligations from the regular marriage. Income tax law does not recognize the fact that he is now paying something like $1,700 or $1,800 a year under a court order made by a provincial judge in Nova Scotia. This was a court order in favour of the common law wife and the two children of the first relationship. It shook me up, I must say, because I thought, given the circumstances of a court order and given the circumstances of a regular liaison that had terminated, that there should somehow be some income tax relief. I checked into it by asking a question the other day of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) and having his reply. Then I suddenly realized that the income tax law is deficient in this respect.
I say deficient because I always thought we had been told in this House that the income tax law was not one that drew moral lines on situations where a buck was a buck was a buck. If you earned it by prostitution, then you were still in a situation where you were gainfully employed. You might have been employed distastefully, but you were gainfully employed and had to make your fair accounting toward the nation's revenues.
1 hope, if I am a little short in my question or the statement of the question involved, that nobody will look at the parliamentary secretary if he has to be a little long with his answer. But we should have an answer. As I say, I thought we had solved this problem a number of years ago when we dealt with income tax reform. Obviously we have not done so.
I simply make the argument that where a court of the land has made an order against a person requiring that person to pay to another person a certain amount of money for the

upkeep of the children of a relationship that has broken down, then due regard should be had to that at income tax time.
May I also make this argument, Mr. Speaker, and through you to the parliamentary secretary, and also through you, Mr. Speaker, to the country, that if we are going to draw any puritanical or moral differentiations between regular marriages which have broken down and the phenomenon of the sixties and the seventies, namely, common law relationships- while common law relationships have existed in the past I think they are much more common now than they used to be- then God help us all.
I once appeared before the Appeal Court of Nova Scotia to argue before Their Lordships that there was a vast difference between what I call a common law relationship where two people were free to marry but had chosen not to and instead lived together-that is, they had gone through no regular civil form of marriage-and a relationship which is called common law where couples live together but one is not free to marry. I pointed out to Their Lordships that this constituted the state of being a concubine and a paramour. After they had recovered their breath at this remarkable fact and had checked their ancient law books, they found out that I was telling it exactly like it was.
I am not dealing with concubines and paramours tonights; I am dealing with what is strictly and factually a common law relationship which has broken up. If I had to deal with the other situation, then I would make the same claim. Where there are court orders in effect and a relationship has clearly been established, then there should also be income tax relief. I hope the heart of the parliamentary secretary is bigger than the treasury, but nevertheless I now await his answer.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bob Kaplan (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: INCOME TAX-EXEMPTIONS FOR MAINTENANCE ORDERS- DISCRIMINATION AGAINST THOSE MADE FOR COMMON LAW SPOUSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have an answer here, but before I begin to give it I want to say that perhaps my heart is bigger that the treasury. The official answer I am about to read, which is a statement in defence of the present legal situation, does not really deter me from reflecting quite positively on the kind of situation to which the hon. member referred, particularly where individuals live together because one of them is not free to translate a common law relationship into a more binding and permanent, legally established relationship.
I want now on behalf of the government to indicate that the income tax treatment of maintenance payments arising out of a common law relationship is one aspect of the matter of appropriate tax treatment of common law relationships.
The tax rules for common law arrangements have presented difficulties for many years. However, as income tax laws must be general in application, they must be based on standards which can be easily identified for administration and enforcement of the law. There is no question of any intention to reflect in our tax laws any moral judgment whatever.
Deductions or exemptions in respect of a spouse are restricted to a legally married spouse because proof of such a marriage is easily obtainable and the spouse is recognized by law for all general purposes. Serious problems would arise in
April 28, 1977

seeking to determine a spouse of a taxpayer on the basis of a period of cohabitation. An effort by officials to identify such a spouse could prove offensive and objectionable to taxpayers who could charge the government with meddling in their private lives.
I wonder if the hon. member might not agree that individuals who choose to live together-and I am talking about those who do have the option of marrying-without the benefit of marriage, may well be opting for a relationship with absolutely no legal implications. Well meaning governments should not deprive them of that right. In a society where the status of
Adjournment Debate
women has legally or virtually reached equality with that of men and is socially moving rapidly toward that desirable goal, it is not unreasonable to regard a common law relationship as a conscious decision of both partners-and again I refer to a relationship in which both partners have the choice of marrying or not-to be treated for all purposes as single individuals.
